Through systematic evaluation of four deployment configurations, we quantify that multi-hop PQC incurs$17-18 ~\text{ms}$latency overhead, exceeding single-hop predictions yet operationally feasible. Critically, Isolation Forest maintains 98.11 % detection accuracy despite PQC-modified traffic, significantly outperforming Random Forest$(94.75 \%, p<0.001)$. These findings establish that networks can adopt quantum-resistant cryptography without compromising threat detection, providing foundations for integrated security architectures. While results are simulation-based, they offer critical insights for guiding realworld PQC-IDS deployments.

title: Q-IoTGuard: Lightweight Quantum Cryptographic Protocols for Resource-Constrained IoT Devices
journal: International Conference on Intelligent Communication Technologies and Virtual Mobile Networks (ICICV)
abs: The explosion of constrained IoT devices with limited resources has increased the necessity of having efficient security measures to counter both the classical and new quantum threat. In this paper, we introduce Q-IoTGuard, a simple quantum cryptography platform that can be used in heterogeneous IoT networks. The model combines entanglement-assisted quantum key distribution (QKD) with lattice-based post-quantum encryption (PQC) in order to guarantee secure communication with a minimum of computational and energy overhead. The methodology commences with data preprocessing, in which the traffic of IoT and characteristics of the devices are organized, standardized and filtered in order to support the efficient cryptographic operations. Raw data is first fed into quantum-assisted key generation with simplified BB84 protocols with error correction and privacy amplification. Lightweight PQC encrypts then message providing resistance against quantum-enabled attacks. The simulation outcomes show that Q-IoTGuard has a low-key generation time, low latency, low-energy consumption, and high quantum attack resistance among sensors, actuators, and gateway devices. The flow-based architecture, which incorporates preprocessing, key gen, and lightweight encryption would make the framework practical to be deployed on resource-constrained IoT devices. Q-IoTGuard is a new scalable and energy-efficient system of securing next-generation IoT networks that addresses the gap between theoretical quantum security and the practical implementation.

title: A Novel Quantum-Resilient Proxy Re-encryption for UAV-to-Cloud Communication
journal: International Conference on Computational Intelligence Approaches and Applications (ICCIAA)
abs: UAVs are increasingly deployed in mission-critical IoT applications (e.g., surveillance, disaster response, environ-mental monitoring) to securely relay sensitive data to cloud infrastructures for storage and analysis, but conventional end-to-end encryption is often too costly for resource-constrained UAVs and may not withstand emerging quantum-capable threats. We propose a quantum-resistant proxy re-encryption (QR-PRE) scheme for UAV-to-cloud communication, where mission data are encrypted with a lightweight symmetric key and then safely re-encrypted by intermediate gateways via proxy cryptography without exposing plaintext. For long-term confidentiality, the framework uses lattice-based post-quantum primitives (Ky-ber512/768) to generate proxy keys and perform re-encryption, providing strong protection against quantum attacks, alongside energy-aware gateway scheduling to reduce swarm overhead while supporting forward secrecy and scalability. Tests on a heterogeneous UAV─gateway─cloud setup show 99.87

title: Shor's Algorithm on NISQ Quantum Hardware: Experimental 4--12-Bit Factorizations and Post-Quantum Cryptography Implications
journal: ICEENG International Conference for Innovations in Intelligent Computing and Cybersecurity (IICC)
abs: Shor's quantum factoring algorithm threatens RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, yet the operational limits of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware for complete Shor implementations remain poorly characterized. This paper presents the first systematic experimental evaluation of the full QFT-based Shor period-finding circuit --- with base a and period r pre-selected classically but the complete inverse-QFT structure fully preserved on hardware --- across nine semiprimes ranging from 4 to 12 bits, executed on IBM 156-qubit Heron-class processors. All nine instances were factored successfully, including the first reported 8--12-bit superconducting results: N = 205 (61.5%) through N = 3427 (73.4%). The central finding is that QFT peak separability (∆K) dominates success probability (R2 = 0.94), while transpilation overhead is essentially irrelevant (R2 = 0.06). Period r = 4 emerges as a noise-robust configuration at 8--12-bit scale, with ∆K >= 8 defining the practical NISQ threshold. Six quantitative design rules enable systematic instance pre-screening, with implications for post-quantum cryptography migration timelines discussed.

title: Sovereign AI for Sustainable Smart Cities: Energy-Aware Distributed Intelligence and Responsible Autonomy
journal: ICEENG International Conference for Innovations in Intelligent Computing and Cybersecurity (IICC)
abs: Smart cities are evolving into complex socio-technical organisms in which artificial intelligence (AI) is embedded into transportation systems, energy grids, healthcare infrastructure, public security operations, and municipal governance mechanisms. Although centralized cloud-based AI architectures have historically powered urban digital systems, the accelerating expansion of critical AI workloads exposes nations to geopolitical dependency, privacy vulnerabilities, and escalating energy and carbon demands. This study proposes a sovereign AI framework for sustainable smart cities rooted in energy-aware distributed intelligence, post-quantum cryptography, constitutional AI oversight, and human-in-the-loop governance. The proposed architecture integrates national AI sovereign clouds, renewable-powered edge clusters, and micro-edge inference nodes coordinated through constitutional rule-based decision engines and verifiable civic audit trails. Through extensive analytical modeling, policy synthesis, and comparative regional case analysis involving Egypt, the GCC, Africa, the European Union (EU), and Singapore, this study demonstrates that sovereign AI architectures can reduce CO2 emissions by up to 87.9 percent while improving system latency by 83 percent and strengthening cybersecurity resilience, ethical accountability, and national strategic autonomy. The results confirm sovereign AI as a foundational paradigm for protecting digital independence, ecological sustainability, infrastructural resilience, and human dignity in twenty-first-century urban environments.

title: A Reinforcement Learning-based Framework for Secure and Efficient IoT Network Traffic Analysis
journal: International Conference on Computer Networks and Inventive Communication Technologies (ICCNCT)
abs: The fast growth of the heterogeneous Internet of Things (IoT) deployments allows placing resource-constrained devices even at a greater risk due to more advanced cyber threats. In one project, this paper is introduced as an entrusted AI-based cybersecurity framework integrating Deep Belief Network (DBN)-based extraction of features, LSTM-based anomaly detection with time, reinforced learning-based adaptive response, and light-weight post-quantum encryption in order to communicate securely. The DBN eliminates the noise in high-dimensional telemetry, and the LSTM models the sequential nature of device behaviour to detect the zero-day and stealthy behaviour with higher sensitivity. The embedded reinforcement learning agent chooses the most efficient mitigation strategies based on finding the trade-offs between latency, the amount of energy used and the level of threat in different IoT settings. Post-quantum cryptography enhances the resistance to future quantum attacks without responsible resource consumption. Through experimental analysis, IoT benchmark datasets illustrate enhanced detection precision, threat containment rate, and resistance to adversarial evasion as compared to conventional methods.

title: From Public Key Infrastructure to Post-Quantum Cryptography: The SECURED Approach
abs: Cryptographic services underpin trust across modern digital systems, from enterprise and industrial infrastructure to cloud platforms, embedded devices, critical communications, and public-sector services. As the computing landscape progressively moves toward the quantum era, this trust model must be re-evaluated in light of new cryptanalytic capabilities and long-term security requirements. The migration from classical public key infrastructure to post-quantum cryptography is therefore a broad systems challenge, although defence and military environments must act earliest because they combine long platform lifecycles, difficult upgrade paths, intermittent connectivity, and (confidential) information lifetime measured in decades. This paper argues that post-quantum migration should be treated as an architectural transformation rather than a simple algorithm replacement. Building on a solid baseline and extending it with recent standards and scientific literature, it identifies crypto agility, hybridisation, and interoperability with legacy infrastructure as the core transition requirements, explains why lattice-based algorithms presently offer the most practical deployment path, and highlights the remaining assurance gap between implementing countermeasures and proving that they work. The paper presents the SECURED approach as a three-pillar architecture composed of a hardware-augmented QRTrusted Computing Base, a deployable PQC SDK for commodity systems, and a cloud PQC-as-a-Service model for protecting the full computing continuum.

title: Hardware Optimisation Research for Post-Quantum Key Exchange Algorithms on Heterogeneous Computing Platforms
journal: International Conference on Sensor-Cloud and Edge Computing System (SCECS)
abs: Quantum computing technology is advancing rapidly, posing a significant threat to existing cipher systems and making the efficient use of post-quantum key exchange algorithms a critical issue. The present paper proposes a hardware acceleration scheme based on a GPU-FPGA heterogeneous computing platform. By analyzing the algorithm's parallelism in depth and combining it with a co-optimization technique for heterogeneous systems, we can efficiently process the key exchange process. A multi-level parallel architecture design and a dedicated hardware optimization unit are adopted to systematically address the algorithm's computational bottleneck. Results from the experiment show that the proposed scheme can process 42,600 transactions per second using the Kyber1024 algorithm. In comparison, the traditional CPU implementation can only process 1,950 transactions per second, with an average processing delay of 0.386 ms. It also has a significant advantage in terms of energy efficiency ratio. In fact, it is 2.8 times higher than the single GPU solution and 2.1 times higher than the single FPGA solution. Research results significantly improve the performance of post-quantum cryptosystems. They provide a new technical route for engineering deployment and lay the groundwork for future widespread applications in areas such as mobile communications and the Internet of Things.

title: AI Driven Crypto Agility Framework for Automated Post Quantum Migration in Critical Infrastructure
journal: International Conference on Modern Computing, Networking and Applications (MCNA)
abs: Post-quantum migration in critical infrastructure is constrained less by algorithm selection than by discovery, dependency analysis, change windows, and rollback safety. This paper presents an implementation-oriented framework for that problem. The design combines parser-first discovery, schemaconstrained retrieval-assisted extraction, evidence reconciliation, a crypto-asset graph, transparent priority scoring, compatibility checks, and staged rollout with rollback. AI is restricted to evidence normalization, candidate-package preparation, and compatibility summarization. Deterministic policy, signed approvals, and maintenance-window controls govern every production action. The paper also specifies an on-premises and air-gapped deployment profile, explicit conflict handling for low-confidence evidence, and a sizing analysis grounded in finalized NIST parameter sizes and public deployment signals available through March 2026. The contribution is a policy-bounded control plane and an evaluation path for critical infrastructure migration, not a claim of autonomous operation or sector-wide deployment.

title: Predictive Security Analytics for Post Quantum Migration Using Digital Twin Simulations
journal: International Conference on Modern Computing, Networking and Applications (MCNA)
abs: Post-quantum migration has become a sequencing problem that spans network edges, certificate ecosystems, signing pipelines, and nonagile hardware. This paper presents a digital twin framework for ranking migration actions before operational rollout. The twin models assets and trust dependencies as a typed graph, separates confidentiality exposure from authentication exposure, and attaches an explicit friction term for packet growth, verifier limits, supplier lag, and maintenance constraints. To reduce calibration ambiguity, the paper defines a transparent cost model based on blast radius, validation burden, supplier lead time, hardware dependence, and maintenance window scarcity. The framework is instantiated with public evidence through early April 2026, cross checked against a recent enterprise cloud transition study, and stress tested with a reproducible sensitivity analysis. The resulting action order is stable in one important respect: hybrid ML-KEM on exposed confidentiality paths is usually the first high value move, while certificate tooling, code signing, and legacy roots of trust determine the longer critical path.

title: Poster Abstract: Hybrid Post-Quantum TLS on Resource-Constrained UAV Platforms
journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Embedded Artificial Intelligence and Sensing Systems - Posters and Demos (SenSys-Adjunct)
abs: The advent of cryptographically relevant quantum computers poses a fundamental threat to classical public-key cryptography. This poster examines whether NIST-standardised post-quantum cryptography (PQC) can be deployed on resource-constrained embedded platforms via a hybrid TLS 1.3 design. We implement and evaluate a complete system combining ML-KEM (Kyber) key encapsulation with ML-DSA (Dilithium) digital signatures atop standard TLS 1.3 on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX within a UAV-based infrastructure inspection scenario. Across three Kyber security levels, hybrid session establishment incurs $1.5 \times-3.7 \times$ overhead ($\mathbf{1 8 - 4 3 ~ m s}$ vs. $\mathbf{1 2 ~ m s}$ baseline), whilst sustained throughput drops by $3.7 \times-5.8 \times(\mathbf{0. 8 2 - 0. 5 2 ~ M B / s}$ vs. $3.01 \text{MB} / \mathrm{s}$). A central finding is that hybrid signing dominates end-to-end cost: over a mission transfer of 30 MB, signing consumes $16.1-17.8 ~\mathrm{s}$ versus $3.9-4.3 ~\mathrm{s}$ for encryption, a roughly $4 \times$ disparity. These results demonstrate that PQC deployment on embedded IoT platforms is feasible even under concurrent onboard inference workloads, and identify signature-path optimisation as the principal lever for improving practical performance.

title: LEAH: Lightweight and Efficient Hardware Accelerator for Code-Based PQC Scheme HQC
journal: 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Hardware Oriented Security and Trust (HOST)
abs: The advent of quantum computing poses a significant threat to modern cryptography. To address this challenge, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has initiated the Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) standardization process, with several algorithms being selected for standardization, including the recent code-based scheme HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic). Meanwhile, a good number of research works in the field have switched to efficient hardware acceleration for PQC schemes. Following this trend, in this paper, we present a novel PQC hardware acceleration work, i.e., a Lightweight and Efficient hardware Accelerator for HQC (LEAH). Our design consists of three innovative hardware architectures for Key Generation, Encapsulation, and Decapsulation of HQC, respectively, while supporting all security levels. In total, we have proposed three layers of contributions, including: (i) dedicated design processes to obtain highly optimized major components for HQC, i.e., sparse polynomial multiplier, sampler, encoder, and decoder; (ii) novel data flow arrangement to design three operational phases of HQC that supports all parameter sets; (iii) a detailed comparison based on Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) implementation to showcase the significant efficiency of the proposed design over the competing ones, e.g., Decapsulation architecture has at least$\mathbf{1 3. 6 6 \%}$(at most$\mathbf{4 9. 8 7 \%}$) less Equivalent Area-Delay Product (EADP) than the existing ones. We hope this outcome can facilitate the deployment of HQC in various applications and impact the ongoing NIST PQC standardization.

title: A Hybrid Secure Communication Architecture Using Quantum Key Distribution and Post Quantum Cryptography
abs: The emergence of highly developed quantum computing is threatening the current established public key cryptography systems like Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) and RSA, and it enables attackers to perpetrate harvest now, decrypt later attacks on the current encrypted communications. Quantum resistant security has provided shedding light on quantum threats by introducing Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) project and Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). QKD offers a no-d efficiency protection with respect to quantum mechanics, though PQC provides protection against quantum attacks of comparable scalability via classical methods of cryptography that are standardized by the NIST. Nevertheless, these two approaches have practical constraints in the field of application in isolation, especially distance, cost, scaling, and infrastructure overhead. This paper suggests a hybrid secure communication system integrating QKD based key generation following the BB84 protocol through the quantum channel and PQC based authentication and integrity schemes following the classical channel and a bulk data transmission scheme utilizing the symmetric encryption. System level performance measures are as well evaluated by simulation to analyse classical cryptography, PQC alone, QKD alone and hybrid$\text{QKD}-\text{PQC}$schemes, comparing the systems throughput and performance impact amid various network conditions. According to the outcomes of the experiment, the proposed hybrid approach injects a throughput overhead of less than 0.1 percent compared to the traditional cryptographic systems, and thus, strong quantum-resilient security is computable with insignificantly low performance costs. This justifies the practicability of hybrid QKD-PQC topologies to prospective quantum safe communication networks encompassing next generation and large-scale distributed communication systems.

title: Trident: Efficient FPGA Acceleration of XMSS Tree in Post-Quantum Signature Scheme SLH-DSA
journal: 2026 IEEE 34th Annual International Symposium on Field-Programmable Custom Computing Machines (FCCM)
abs: The emergence of quantum computing poses significant threats to conventional cryptographic systems, necessitating the efficient hardware acceleration of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), especially on the Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) platforms. SPHINCS+, recently standardized by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) as SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), represents the only hash-based digital signature scheme. Its practical deployment, however, is restricted by computationally intense operations, particularly in the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS) tree, where WOTS+ (Winternitz One-Time Signature Plus) public key generation consumes the majority of signature generation cycles. With this background, this paper presents Trident, an innovative FPGA-based hardware accelerator that addresses critical performance and resource challenges in XMSS of SLH-DSA. First, we propose a triangle hash unit architecture that enables parallel execution of up to three hash operations simultaneously, directly addressing the computational bottleneck in XMSS tree construction and WOTS+ chain operations. Second, we develop an optimized memory caching scheme that reduces on-chip memory requirements via intermediate value management. Third, we implement the Trident on FPGAs and comprehensively evaluate it across all parameter sets at multiple security levels, i.e., up to 8.6× improvement in signature generation and up to 5.4× speed-up in verification operations. Extended Hypertree evaluation shows a 34.6× area-delay product (ADP) improvement on UltraScale+ FPGA for SLH-DSA-128s. This Trident represents a significant advancement toward practical SLH-DSA deployment in FPGA environments.

title: Introduction to Post Quantum Cryptography for Resource Constrained Systems
abs: With the advent and quick improvement of quantum computers, conventional cryptographic systems will become vulnerable in the near future, creating a high risk in security and privacy. For this reason, post quantum cryptographic schemes have been developed which impose new hardware and software requirements to existing and upcoming hardware. While there are several works in the literature focused on post quantum cryptography acceleration in general purpose, high performance systems, the vast majority of computing devices, i.e. embedded, Internet of Things are not covered by them, due to their high area, power or memory cost. In this tutorial, we will focus on the particular case of these devices. The tutorial includes the active standardization activities in various bodies particularly focused on RISC-V, as well as on-going efforts in European Commission funded research projects, such as PQC4eMRTD and SMARTY.

title: A Chosen-Ciphertext Side-Channel Attack on Protected ML-KEM Using Pairwise Bit-Flipping
abs: Post-quantum cryptography addresses the threat posed by large-scale quantum computers to current public-key cryptosystems. After an eight-year evaluation process, NIST has standardized ML-KEM, a quantum-resistant scheme for publickey encryption and key encapsulation, whose global deployment is anticipated by 2035. Beyond algorithmic security, the resistance of physical implementations of ML-KEM to sidechannel attacks is important for a secure transition. This paper evaluates the resistance of a software implementation of MLKEM protected against side-channel analysis using masking and shuffling. Despite these countermeasures, we can recover the secret key using only one third of the traces compared to the state-of-the-art attack. Our main contribution is a novel chosenciphertext construction method that 1) circumvents the shuffling countermeasure, and 2) overcomes the inter-device variation problem. This method is applicable not only to ML-KEM, but also to other lattice-based PKE or KEM algorithms. We provide an in-depth analysis of the attack methodology, validate the attack on an ARM Cortex-M4 platform recommended by NIST for benchmarking, and suggest potential countermeasures for hardening ML-KEM implementations against side-channel attacks.

title: Accelerated Packet Forwarding for Quantum-Secured Communications
abs: Quantum-secure communication systems impose new performance constraints on networked systems due to the computational overhead entailed within primitives of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) in terms of key composition and exchange, particularly affecting latency-sensitive environments consisting of resource-constrained devices. Hence, the need for deploying PQC over programmable dataplanes such as to accelerate secure session initiation and pragmatically reduce device and network-level computational overheads is real. In this paper we provide work-in-progress results assessing network packet acceleration techniques in PQC-enabled sessions by comparing the standard TCP socket implementation against kernel-assisted Packet-MMAP forwarding and zero-copy shared memory ring buffer. The results of this study highlight that the zero-copy forwarding approach can significantly improve packet processing performance over conventional socket-based implementations. In addition, we indicate device-level performance with respect to their power management state.

title: Q-FLAP: Quantum-Secured Federated Learning with Adaptive Protection for Jamming-Resilient LEO Satellite-IoT Networks
abs: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations face two converging threats, adaptive jamming that learns defensive behavior and quantum computers capable of breaking today's cryptography. To address this, we propose Q-FLAP, a unified framework that integrates quantum-secured federated learning (FL) with deep reinforcement learning (DRL), to address both challenges. Q-FLAP models anti-jamming channel selection as a distributed Markov decision process, where satellites learn policies via Deep Q-Networks while federated averaging enables coordination without centralizing sensitive data. Federated updates are secured using BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) and lattice-based post-quantum cryptography (PQC), ensuring resilience against classical eavesdropping and harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks. Analytical results establish a steady-state throughput benchmark under adversarial jamming. Simulations show that under intelligent jamming, Q-FLAP retains 78% of nominal capacity, achieving 2.52 Gbps raw throughput and a 77.9% transmission success rate. Security overhead is minimal, 2.16% for QKD and 0.094% for PQC, yielding effective secure throughputs of 2.46 Gbps and 2.52 Gbps. Compared with baseline methods, Q-FLAP improves throughput by 2.5 times over random allocation and 1.67 times over greedy channel selection.

title: Accelerating the Post-Quantum Transition: A GPU-Based Performance Comparison of ML-KEM and ML-DSA
journal: International Conference on Current Trends in Advanced Computing (ICCTAC)
kw: NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)
abs: As National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST) moves towards completing its Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) standards (FIPS 203 ML-KEM & FIPS 204 ML-DSA), it leaves the cloud security industry with a complex, yet unavoidable challenge. These new lattice-based algorithms are designed to combat attacks from quantum computers, but they do come with a price. The performance degradation will be significant as well as impacting the overall infrastructure. To understand the impact of NIST's new algorithms we performed a benchmarking study to see how each of them compare side-by-side over multiple NIST security levels with an emphasis on the resources they consume and time taken to perform each operation. As expected, we found that both algorithms have a large amount of overhead due to their computational processes (specifically using Number Theoretic Transform and rejection sampling) which, while not necessarily apparent to end-users, are a factor users should be aware of. One thing we did not do in our testing is to only test in an ideal laboratory environment rather we also created a hybrid test system consisting of an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and an NVIDIA H100 (to closely resemble a real-world modern cloud setup). Although there was a lot of variance in the results, ML-KEM yielded the best overall effectiveness, particularly due to its lower resource utilization (compared to ML-DSA) and optimized for high-volume key exchange very well. The challenge is still figuring out how to implement and implement correctly; that will require further research in the future.

title: Quantum Machine Learning for Cyber Threat Intelligence: A Scoping Review of Current Capabilities and Future Directions
journal: 2026 22nd IEEE International Colloquium on Signal Processing & Its Applications (CSPA)
abs: Emerging cyber threats demand novel detection and analysis paradigms that classical machine learning approaches are increasingly unable to address at requisite scale and speed. Quantum Machine Learning (QML), leveraging quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition and entanglement, has emerged as a promising framework for cyber threat intelligence (CTI). This scoping review systematically examines 24 published works from 2020 to 2025 following the PRISMA-ScR protocol. We classify QML frameworks like Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVM), Quantum Neural Networks (QNN), Variational Quantum Circuits (VQC), and Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks (QCNN) across four primary CTI domains: intrusion detection, malware classification, anomaly detection, and phishing detection. Results show that QML models achieved up to 98% accuracy in intrusion detection and 97% in IoT anomaly detection on curated benchmark datasets. Critical caveats apply: 83.3% of studies relied exclusively on quantum simulators rather than real hardware, most benchmarks used datasets predating 2017, and the classical pre-processing and post-processing overheads in hybrid architectures substantially qualify reported speedup claims. We assess hardware constraints in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, data encoding bottlenecks, and missing quality benchmarks. NIST post-quantum cryptography standards (FIPS 203-205, August 2024) and IBM quantum hardware milestones are discussed as contextual anchors. A structured research agenda concludes the review.

title: Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation Mechanisms: A Comparative Review of ML-KEM, BIKE, and HQC
journal: 2026 22nd IEEE International Colloquium on Signal Processing & Its Applications (CSPA)
abs: Large-scale quantum computers will fundamentally compromise public-key cryptosystems based on integer factorization and the discrete logarithm problem. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) standardized ML-KEM (FIPS 203, August 2024) and selected HQC (March 2025) as a code-based backup Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM). This paper presents a structured comparative analysis of ML-KEM, BIKE (Bit Flipping Key Encapsulation), and HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic) across six dimensions: mathematical foundations, key and ciphertext sizes, computational performance with explicit instruction-set architecture (ISA) attribution, quantitative security margins, side-channel resistance, and TLS 1.3 handshake overhead. A phased migration roadmap is also provided. ML-KEM delivers compact key material, formally proven Indistinguishability under Adaptive Chosen Ciphertext Attack (IND-CCA2) security, and balanced performance, making it the appropriate primary KEM for general deployment. HQC supplies a formally bounded Decryption Failure Rate (DFR) and mathematical independence from lattice assumptions, establishing it as a sound standardized backup. BIKE offers competitive encapsulation speed but relies on an empirically bounded, rather than formally proven, DFR, constituting a residual security gap that precluded its standardization.

title: Post-Quantum Secure Communication on Resource-Constrained UAVs for Mission-Critical Infrastructure Protection
abs: The use of UAVs in mission-critical applications requires strict implementation of resilient security mechanisms in the medium and long term. This objective can only be achieved by implementing cryptographic primitives that are resistant to quantum attacks. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms have recently been standardized, but their performance and resource requirements on constrained devices have not been thoroughly investigated. This paper proposes an optimized architecture for the use of drone swarms in mission-critical applications, a lightweight Signed Post-Quantum Key Exchange Protocol suitable for limited processing resources, and a quantitative analysis based on experiments for selecting suitable PQC primitives. The results obtained indicate that the integration of PQC into UAV systems is feasible.

title: A Quantum-Agile Framework for Secure 5G Core Communication Using Post-Quantum TLS
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: The rise of quantum computing poses a critical threat to current cryptographic protocols, particularly RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), which are vulnerable to attacks such as Shor's algorithm. As 5G networks rely heavily on public key infrastructure, the risk of compromise in the quantum era is significant. Transitioning to post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) primitives is therefore an urgent priority. This paper presents a practical framework for integrating PQC into 5G control plane communication, specifically over Service-Based Interfaces (SBIs). Using the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) finalist algorithm Dilithium3, we implement PQC-enabled Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshakes via a modular proxy built in Python. The proxy intercepts inter-service traffic and offloads cryptographic operations to a containerized environment using liboqs. Importantly, this integration does not require altering existing 5G functions. System-level metrics, including CPU (Central Processing Unit) usage, memory, latency, and jitter, were benchmarked before and after PQC integration. Results show performance overhead remains within acceptable bounds, confirming deployment viability. This work proposes a hybrid migration strategy that enables backward compatibility and cryptographic agility. It provides a scalable and testable foundation for securing 5G networks in the quantum era while aligning with emerging European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) and NIST guidelines for post-quantum transition.

title: Implementation and transition to post-quantum cryptography of the Minimal IKE protocol
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: This paper concerns the Minimal Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol, which has received little attention to date, despite its potential to make the best-known IKE protocol sufficiently lightweight to be also applied in contexts where it is currently prohibitive, due to its large footprint. First, we introduce and describe Colibri, an efficient, open-source implementation of the Minimal IKE protocol, which allows us to quantitatively assess its real advantages in terms of lightness. Then we introduce a post-quantum variant of the Minimal IKE protocol, which is essential to make it contemporary, and assess it through Colibri. We demonstrate that the protocol performance remains excellent even in such a more challenging context, making it suitable for deploying pervasive and quantum-resistant virtual private networks.

title: NTRU Based Novel Approach to Secure UAV Communications Through MQTT and Blockchain
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: The security of UAV communications is one of the crucial aspects in UAV networks due to the increasing use of UAVs in various applications. In this paper, a novel approach based on Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is proposed to improve the security of UAV communications. The proposed approach utilizes the N-th Degree Truncated Polynomial Ring Unit (NTRU) algorithm, integrated with Blockchain Technology (BT) and the Message Queuing Telemetry Transport Protocol (MQTT). In the proposed approach, UAVs are authenticated by the server, and the BT ledger stores the UAV information, such as its identification number and public key. The encryption and decryption of the message is performed using a securely established secret key between the sender and the receiver UAV. The results of the proposed approach are evaluated and compared with other existing PQC algorithms. The results show that the proposed approach is more computationally efficient and faster than other algorithms.

title: PQ-TabNet: A Post-Quantum Secure Framework for Intrusion Detection in UAV Networks
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are used in various civilian applications to collect data. Security is a major issue in UAV networks. To securely transmit the data from the UAVs to the base station, the data must be sent in encrypted form. Cryptography techniques are used for encryption and decryption. Classical cryptography schemes do not provide protection against quantum attacks. To secure the data from quantum threats we use post quantum cryptography(PQC) techniques. In this paper, a post-quantum secure intrusion detection model named the PQ-TabNet model is proposed to address these challenges. The proposed model integrates N-th Degree Truncated Polynomial Ring unit (NTRU) lattice-based encryption with a transformer-based deep learning model to ensure confidentiality and resilience against both classical and quantum attacks. The proposed model was trained on the CICIDS2018 data set, where PQ-TabNet achieved better performance than the Kyber-based configuration in terms of energy efficiency and latency. Experimental analysis demonstrated that NTRU provided faster encryption and reduced energy consumption while maintaining strong quantum resistance.

title: Q-SAFe:Quantum-Safe Agentic Federated Learning Scheme for Telemedicine Edge Networks
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong potential in clinical reasoning, but their scale and cost prevent deployment on resource-constrained telemedicine edge networks. Small language models (SLMs) offer efficiency, yet their limited semantic depth hinders accurate diagnostic support. This gap motivates a Federated Learning (FL) approach, where distributed SLMs collaborate under supervision, while Knowledge Distillation (KD) transfers reasoning from LLMs to sustain accuracy. However, today's SLM deployments still lack agentic coordination, leaving clinical workflows fragmented. Agentic communication security relies on classical cryptography that cannot withstand quantum adversaries. To address these challenges, we proposeQ-SAFe, a four-phase scheme that integrates federated SLM training, agentic orchestration, and Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) algorithms. Patient and hospital agents are registered, and are collaboratively trained with Federated Proximal (FedProx) and KD strategy. They are connected through authenticated cross-layer handshakes, and protected by Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) scheme for secure record exchange. Validations show thatQ-SAFesustains clinical-grade responsiveness (≤ 200 ms latency under 300 users), achieves stable convergence (≈ 85% accuracy within 50 rounds), and imposes only 3 KB per-exchange cryptographic overhead, making it suitable for practical edge deployments. The code is available athttps://github.com/Mahdiya-Nishat/Q-SAFe.

title: Performance of NIST Post-quantum Cryptography Additional Digital Signature Algorithms
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: NIST post-quantum cryptography (PQC) project selected three digital signature algorithms (Dilithium, Falcon, and SPHINCS+) to standardize as PQC digital signature standards. In addition to the PQC digital signature standards, for diversity and to address the concerns on the overheads including key/signature sizes and computational performances, NIST is considering 14 additional digital signature algorithms for further standardization. One or more algorithms from these 14 algorithms can be selected for further standardization. However due to the dynamic nature of the NIST standardization process and cryptanalysis, all these candidate algorithms go through continuous changes and updates. The latest updates in Oct 2025 outdated the previous performance analyses of these algorithms. In this paper, we study the computational performance overheads of the NIST PQC additional signature candidates (round 2 - latest submission packages) in terms of key generation time, signing time, and verification time. Our results show that additional signature candidate algorithms including Hawk, CROSS, and SNOVA are competitive and computationally outperform the PQC standards on several occasions.

title: Attack Path Inferences for Quantum-Safe FutureG Network Security
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: The looming advent of "Q-Day" is urging standardization agencies to overhaul current cryptographic methods like RSA and Diffie-Hellman in favor of two quantum-safe solutions: post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD). FutureG will utilize a hybrid PQC-QKD approach to safeguard data as well as provide quantum computing as a cloud-based service (QCaaS) in this new era of computing. To address the limited literature on quantum-safe FutureG network penetration testing, this paper presents a systematic cybersecurity analysis framework. First, we extend MulVAL, an open source framework for generating logical attack graphs, to include vulnerabilities related to PQC, QKD, and QCaaS within a FutureG context. Next, using the extended MulVAL, we construct an attack graph for a quantum-safe FutureG network, convert it into a Markov Decision Process (MDP), and implement multiple reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms on the resulting MDP model, including Q-Learning, SARSA, DQN, PPO, A2C, and TRPO. Lastly, we evaluate and compare these RL algorithms based on the rolling average reward and cumulative reward metrics, and analyze the inferred attack paths in relation to the shortest attack trace and the RL algorithms.

title: A Novel Attack-Aware Adaptive Encryption Architecture for Quantum Resilient Networks
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: Next-generation networks, including IoT, edge, vehicular, and 6G systems, require cryptographic schemes that not only resist attacks but also withstand channel degradation without disrupting secure data flows. This paper presents a novel adaptive encryption architecture for quantum-resilient networks that integrates real-time attack detection in quantum channels with per frame key management. A lightweight controller has been designed, which tracks the quantum bit error rate (QBER) via a sliding-window hysteresis and buffer thresholds, deciding per frame whether to derive symmetric keys from Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) or from a post-quantum cryptographic fallback, while maintaining a unified AES─GCM AEAD dataplane. Moreover, a deterministic HMAC-based key derivation function (HKDF) schedule binding eliminates key reuse across modes, retransmissions, and re-encapsulations. Experimental evaluation on image payloads shows: (i) timely QBER-spike detection with 9.5-frame latency and zero misses; (ii) full decryptability and tamper detection across both key sources; (iii) symmetric throughput of ≈ 1.1GB/s with negligible adaptation overhead; and (iv) near-ideal ciphertext metrics including entropy 8.02bits/pixel, NPCR ≈ 99.6%, and UACI ≈ 30.7%. The framework achieves secure, continuous encryption by preventing unsafe QKD use and maintaining authenticated operation under quantum-channel degradation.

title: Channel-Adaptive Post-Quantum Cryptography for Secure and Efficient Non-Terrestrial Networks
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTNs), including satellite systems, are increasingly integrated with 5G/6G to ensure global connectivity. Existing research largely relies on classical cryptography adapted to NTN contexts, but such schemes are vulnerable to quantum-based attacks. Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) offers quantum-safe security, yet its computational and bandwidth overheads challenge resource-limited satellite-IoT networks. This paper introduces Channel-Adaptive Post-uantum NTN Security (CA-PQNTN), an adaptive, channel-aware PQC framework that dynamically tunes cryptographic parameters based on link quality and data sensitivity. A detailed system model combining PQC agility with energy consumption analysis is developed for satellite-IoT environments. Simulation results show that CA-PQNTN improves packet delivery rate by approximately 11.5%, reduces energy consumption by 24.9%, and lowers bandwidth overhead by 26.6% compared to static PQC, with only a modest drop in average security (192-bit vs. 256-bit). The framework maintains quantum resilience while intelligently balancing security and efficiency for future NTNs.

title: Security Evaluations of Post-Quantum Cryptographic Primitives Against Quantum and AI-Based Attacks
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: The emergence of quantum computing poses an existential threat to conventional cryptographic systems, prompting the development of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) based on quantum-resistant mathematical problems. However, the long-term security of these primitives remains uncertain, especially under realistic quantum and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven attack scenarios. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of the security of PQC primitives with a dual focus: (i) analyzing advances in quantum algorithms that target the underlying hardness assumptions of lattice-based, code-based, and other post-quantum schemes; and (ii) leveraging AI-based methodologies for identifying cryptographic vulnerabilities. We survey the current state of quantum cryptanalysis, propose a unified insights for evaluations. Our findings offer updated parameter recommendations and highlight both strengths and potential fragilities in leading PQC candidates. The results contribute actionable insights toward the design and standardization of resilient cryptographic systems for the post-quantum era.

title: QuantOnion: Quantum assisted Onion Routing for Trusted Data Sharing underlying 6G networks
journal: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abs: Sixth-generation (6G) networks transmit massive traffic over open channels, exposing data to interception that threatens anonymity and confidentiality. Onion routing (OR) addresses these risks by obscuring communication paths and protecting user identities. However, conventional OR frameworks faces the challenge of quantum adversaries. Thus, post-quantum cryptography (PQC) offers quantum-resistant security with improved scalability. Thus, the paper presents a novel framework,QuantOnionthat enhances OR key sharing and signing with NIST standardized PQC schemes. The scheme integrates two module lattice (ML) PQC algorithms, namely, the key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) for OR sessions, and the digital signature algorithm (DSA) for message authentication. These algorithms operate over a lightweight blockchain (lightchain) that enforces real-time identity verification and session logging in resource-constrained TOR networks, followed by ethereum smart contracts to enforce tamper-proof policy compliance and access control with the system. The framework is tested for PQC analysis, blockchain network analysis, and computation and communication costs. Our experimental evaluation demonstrated an average improvement of approximately 85-90% in both key generation latency and digital signature operations compared to classical RSA/ECC and traditional DSA schemes while reducing the probability of quantum attacks to negligible levels < 10−6. These results underscore the significant potential of our approach to secure high-volume, low-latency communications in the quantum era.

title: Post-Quantum Federated Zero-Trust Authentication Framework for Ultra-Dense 6G Network Slicing Using Lattice-Based Cryptography
journal: International Conference on Computational Robotics, Testing and Engineering Evaluation (ICCRTEE)
abs: The high-performance needed to ensure QoS optimization and a high level of security required by 6 G network slicing is ultra-dense. Nevertheless, the current authentication systems including PKI, ECC, and 5G-AKA are not quantum-resistant and commonly create scaling and latency issues in distributed systems. To meet these demands, this paper presents a Post-Quantum Federated Zero-Trust (PQ-ZT) model, which combines lattice-based cryptography and federated QoS prediction. The model can be used to achieve privacy-preserving distributed learning but provide persistently quantum-resistant authentication. Experimental findings show that it predicts 96 % with low MSE and high R2 value and has lower latency of authentication and increased throughput as compared to the traditional schemes. The framework also reduces the packet loss and latency, and the computational overhead is manageable. Even though the real-time implementation in live 6 G testbeds is worked to do, the proposed solution affirms that the concept of integrating post-quantum security with intelligent QoS prediction offers a scalable, secure, and performance-efficient architecture of ultra-dense 6G network slicing conditions.

title: Quantum Resistant Security Using Multivariant Polynomial Cryptography
journal: International Conference on Computational Robotics, Testing and Engineering Evaluation (ICCRTEE)
abs: To create an AI-assisted multivariate polynomial cryptography system which can provide secure, efficient, and Quantum resistant communication within modern digital infrastructures and environments. Group 1 evaluated a baseline cryptographic approach using standard encryption and encoding techniques which included Base64 and ROT13 and AES and RSA and a multivariate polynomial-based cryptosystem which used Genetic Algorithm and GradientBased Search for optimization. The team evaluated their performance metrics through encryption time decryption time key length security strength and computational complexity. Group 2 evaluated the performance of a quantum resistant cryptographic algorithm to measure its effectiveness by examining 26 subjects who performed operations using optimized polynomial coefficients and assessed encryption/decryption time, overhead, cipher length/key length, and ability to be scaled in size, as well as resistance to future quantum attacks.Results:An average accuracy of 98.5% has been achieved by the new cryptographic system. This is greater than AES (92.5%), RSA (94.1%) and Kyber (96.8%), with a low standard deviation of 0.95, and all grown statistically significantly better at the level ($\mathbf{p}<0.001$) than any other tested methods. The system will also have very high resistance against quantum computers, have relatively little computational cost, and provide very repeatable results when used repeatedly over long periods of time.Conclusion: The Cryptographic System developed from this study will be an efficient, scalable means of securing communications after quantum computing comes into existence by providing a secure means of protecting the confidentiality of data, maintaining its integrity and ensuring its authenticity from quantum computing attacks.

title: An Integrated Standard-Compliant Framework for UAV Cyber Resilience Using Post-Quantum Cryptography and LSTM-Based Anomaly Detection
journal: 2026 International Conference on Robotics and Automation in Industry (ICRAI)
abs: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are becoming a significant part of numerous systems such as surveillance, disaster response, delivery, and urban air mobility. It remains highly vulnerable to high-tech cyber and physical attacks. The security practices currently in place are fragmented, non-agile, and not fully meeting the international standards. The proposed paper presents a five-layer UAV cybersecurity model with a Trust and Policy Plane to allow real-time monitoring, adaptive response, and ongoing adherence to such standards like NIST CSF 2.0, IEC 62443, DO-326A, and ASTM F3411. The framework is assessed with a real-time UAV telemetry dataset of 69,000 flight samples, in which, threat scenarios involving remote control (RC) signal perturbation and telemetry manipulation, as well as, Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise, are simulated. An anomaly detection model is a Multivariate LSTM Autoencoder with$\mathbf{9 8 \%}$accuracy,$\mathbf{6 0. 1 \%}$precision, 100% recall, and 75.1% F1-score with reduced reconstruction error during training, which is capable of detecting anomalies in a wide range of operating and adversarial conditions.

title: BCRLSecureLink: A Blockchain, Cryptography, and Reinforcement Learning-Based Defense Against Link Discovery Attacks in SDVN
authors: Wijesekara, Patikiri Arachchige Don Shehan Nilmantha
journal: International Symposium on Cluster, Cloud and Internet Computing (CCGrid)
abs: In a Software-Defined Vehicular Network (SDVN), the performance can be drastically affected if the network topology is poisoned by Link Discovery Attacks (LDAs). Because of frequent topology changes with non-adaptive link rediscovery, a lack of distributed node behavioral monitoring and blacklisting without entirely relying on the controller, high communication interception, a lack of authenticity and integrity, and a reliance on single observation, recent solutions can struggle to mitigate LDA in the context of dynamic SDVN LD. In order to respond to this research gap, we first demonstrate 5 LDAs that can exist in a standard SDVN architecture by exploiting the vulnerabilities in location tracking and the LD service. Then, we propose a novel framework to detect LDA by using Q-learning to derive link states by considering the link's suspicious behavior, packet delivery, and latency and with a location-driven adaptive LD technique, while in the process we employ cycle- and non-cyclebased digital signatures with mixed post-quantum and classical cryptography, Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) of Hash Message Authentication Codes (HMACs) stored in the blockchain, time-limited session-based HMACs, packet limiting with signature matching, location verification, and Diffie-Hellman symmetric key issuing to mitigate the attacks. Moreover, a permissioned blockchain is utilized by using one smart contract for node registration using a challenge-response mechanism with DH, public, and global key exchange; subsequent node authentication using signatures, ZKPs, attributes, and HMACs through established encrypted communication; and a second smart contract to maintain non-tamperable node reputation and location scores by monitoring node behavior and maintaining endorser trust scores for weighted reputation updates for consensus-based node blacklisting. The proposed method resulted in the second-best channel utilization under attack 1, the best link discovery latency under attack 2, the best PDR and Matthews Correlation Coefficient, and zero packet interception ratios under attacks 3, 4, and 5 despite its higher computational complexity.

title: Analysis of Recent Developments in Quantum Cryptography: A Comprehensive Review
abs: With a focus on developments from 2020 to 2025, this review examines recent experimental, theoretical, and systems-level developments in quantum cryptography. We focus on progress in photonic integration for continuous-variable (CV) and discrete-variable (DV) quantum key distribution (QKD), measurement-device-independent (MDI) and device-independent (DI) security models, long-distance terrestrial and satellite demonstrations, and progress toward quantum repeaters and a quantum internet. We summarize protocol descriptions, provide equations and finite-key security comments, present representative experimental milestones, and discuss practical integration with classical post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and standards. Finally, we outline open problems and a pragmatic roadmap for near-term deployments.

title: GPU Acceleration of Learning With Errors KEMs Using OpenACC for Post-Quantum Cryptography
abs: Shor's algorithm proved that asymmetric cryptographic protocols based on the integer factorization and discrete logarithm problems are no longer safe in a world with large-scale quantum computers. As a result, Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) has been developed over the last few years, seeking cryptographic primitives resistant to quantum attacks. One of the main hard problems underlying PQC schemes is the Learning with Errors (LWE) problem, which is significantly more computationally intensive than its classical predecessors. In this work, we present a Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) based on plain LWE and develop a GPU-oriented implementation using OpenACC. We evaluate the performance of our accelerated application in terms of both time-to-solution and energy-to-solution, considering bare-metal and containerized executions across multiple NVIDIA GPU models and generations. Our implementation achieves significant acceleration across all tested GPU platforms. In particular, on the NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchip, it attains up to a $208\times$ speedup over a multithreaded CPU baseline and enables the execution of problem sizes that are impractical on CPU architectures due to memory and synchronization constraints. Energy consumption analysis also shows $\approx 2\times$ better efficiency when using the Superchip compared to systems equipped with x86-based CPUs and NVIDIA H100 GPUs. These results highlight the effectiveness of GPU acceleration for computationally demanding LWE-based cryptographic workloads.

title: A Survey on Security with Quantum Computing
abs: Quantum computing has emerged as a transformative computing paradigm capable of solving problems that remain computationally infeasible for classical systems; however, its rapid advancement also introduces significant security, privacy, and reliability concerns. In this context, this survey presents a comprehensive review of security challenges and mitigation strategies associated with quantum computing, focusing on security issues in quantum computers, security threats caused by quantum computers, and security mechanisms developed for quantum systems. The paper examines vulnerabilities in quantum hardware and software, the impact of quantum computing on existing cryptographic infrastructures and cybersecurity mechanisms, and the development of quantum-resilient solutions such as post-quantum cryptography, quantum-safe communication protocols, quantum intrusion detection systems, and quantum-aware software engineering techniques. In addition, the survey discusses emerging applications of quantum technologies in cybersecurity domains, including malware detection, network intrusion detection, Internet of Things (IoT) security, and secure communication systems. Furthermore, the paper analyzes existing quantum error mitigation and fault-tolerance approaches designed to improve the robustness and trustworthiness of quantum computation under realistic noisy conditions. By consolidating recent advances, open research challenges, and future directions, this survey provides a structured overview of the evolving intersection between quantum computing and cybersecurity, while serving as a reference for researchers and practitioners working toward secure, resilient, and quantum-ready computing infrastructures.

title: How To Track Qubits Through Space and Time (Or: Sailing in a Quantum Boat)
abs: While quantum position verification aims to certify a prover's location using quantum information, existing security definitions only guarantee that part of the successful adversarial party is in the claimed location. This leaves open the possibility that a distributed team of adversaries can jointly simulate a prover in a way that defeats the intended meaning of ``being at a location'' in position-based cryptography. We introduce stronger notions of position verification that we call quantum localization, which requires that there is a specified, unclonable state at the verified spacetime point -- and that this state can be found nowhere else. We show that quantum localization leads naturally to a meaningful notion of trajectory verification, in which quantum information is verifiably tracked through space and time. We construct quantum localization and trajectory verification protocols using quantum anchor states, which generalize coset states from unclonable cryptography. The security of our schemes is proven in the classical oracle (i.e. ideal obfuscation) model, which can be heuristically instantiated in the plain model using post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation. We also introduce and instantiate the concept of functionality localization, which guarantees that the adversary has the ability to compute a secret function at the verified spacetime point, and this function cannot be computed anywhere else. This raises the intriguing possibility of localizing computational capabilities in space and time. More broadly, we believe our notions of quantum localization and our feasibility results provide stronger foundations for position-based cryptography.

title: Efficient and Quantum-safe Internet Key Exchange Protocols for Satellite Communications
abs: This paper studies cryptographic key exchange in satellite communications, which requires specific solutions because the satellite context presents unique challenges, particularly concerning onboard resource constraints and long transmission latency. We address these challenges by considering the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol, which is widely used in terrestrial networks, and studying its applicability in the satellite context. This requires addressing two main issues: i) its efficiency in terms of the resources and bandwidth required to adapt to satellite terminals, and ii) its resistance even to attackers equipped with a quantum computer, in order to resist obsolescence and defend against harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks. We study these aspects from both a design and experimental point of view, defining and assessing some protocol variants characterized by low complexity and quantum resistance. To address the need to manage the transition from classic cryptographic primitives to post-quantum ones, we also consider the possibility of using hybrid cryptographic solutions that combine them both.

title: Exact Hidden Paths in Noisy High Dimensional Path Spaces
abs: We introduce a mathematical and cryptographic framework for exact recovery of noisy hidden paths in high dimensional discrete path spaces. The work is inspired by the path integral viewpoint, where global quantities arise from contributions over many possible trajectories. Instead of approximating a global path sum, we study the inverse problem of recovering one exact hidden trajectory from incomplete, noisy, projected, and aggregated observables. The hidden object is a planted discrete path whose transitions may include macro steps, microscopic perturbations, and discrete noise. Public information is represented by large observable vectors rather than short hash digests, since excessive compression would bound the effective recovery problem by the digest size. We formalize several recovery notions, including planted exact recovery, arbitrary witness recovery, canonical recovery, quotient recovery, and recovery of derived encodings. The main distinction is that approximate reconstruction and exact recovery are fundamentally different tasks. A method may reveal coarse geometry or dominant regions without recovering the precise microscopic sequence defining the hidden path. We also discuss attack surfaces relevant to future cryptographic use, including linearization, lattice style recovery, dynamic programming, meet in the middle attacks, SAT and SMT formulations, approximation followed by rounding, witness collisions, and generic quantum search. This work does not claim a complete post quantum cryptosystem. It provides a formal framework for studying exact hidden path recovery as a possible foundation for future cryptographic constructions

title: Operationalising Post Quantum TLS Automated Configuration Profiling and Hybrid PQC Deployment in Financial Infrastructure
abs: Organisations are upgrading their cryptographic infrastructure to become quantum safe before large scale quantum computers materialise. Post quantum cryptography (PQC) standards now exist for key exchange and digital signatures, but the urgent question for adopters is how to operationalise PQC in complex environments with confidence. In banking, Transport Layer Security (TLS), for example, protects data in transit across public facing channels and internal services, and is terminated at many heterogeneous endpoints (web servers, API gateways, load balancers, reverse proxies), each a potential quantum vulnerable component and migration target. We argue that the bottleneck is operational rather than algorithmic, hybrid key exchanges such as MLKEM and hybrid MLKEM key exchanges are already available in mainstream libraries, but security teams lack precise visibility into TLS configurations and repeatable methods for enabling PQC compatible settings across a heterogeneous estate. This paper presents a configuration parsing methodology that automatically extracts and normalises TLS cryptographic posture across dominant enterprise web server stacks, producing a unified, provenance traced cryptographic inventory as a foundation for migration and compliance. We demonstrate the approach on 8,443 real world Nginx configurations from public repositories and in a proof of concept deployment at a financial institution, where MLKEM and hybrid MLKEM key exchanges at TLS termination points (web server and API gateway) securing an internal application, with zero application layer changes and manageable performance overhead.

title: Simple Power Analysis on Post-Quantum Code Based Cryptosystems
abs: Post-Quantum cryptography is about to substitute current cryptographic schemes as being resilient in attacks from quantum computers. McEleiece and Bit Flip Key Encapsulation (BIKE) are two delight representatives based on coding theory where classical structural attacks against these algorithms can be successfully phased out by selecting the appropriate key size. Using low cost equipment, the method of Simple Power Analysis (SPA) is used in this paper to evaluate whether or not there is significant information leakage during the decapsulation phase where the shared secret key is generated. Executing a related experiment it is shown that correlation between electromagnetic emissions and secret values exists. In the aftermath, with only 200 power traces collected, machine learning models can predict secret bits of the shared session key, produced during the decapsulation.

title: quantum-safe: Bridging the Post-Quantum Production Gap with a Hybrid-by-Default Python Cryptography Library
abs: The August 2024 finalisation of FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) closed the algorithmic gap in post-quantum cryptography (PQC). The production gap -- hybrid combiners, versioned key formats, protocol helpers, and migration tooling -- remains open. We present quantum-safe, a Python library that closes all three critical gaps we identify, and a systematic evaluation of the nine-library ecosystem that quantifies them. We score nine PQC libraries across eight production-readiness dimensions. Three dimensions have coverage below 35%: hybrid KEM support (11%), migration tooling (22%), and protocol integration (33%). quantum-safe scores Full on all eight. The full API reduces the hybrid KEM task from 45 lines of manual combiner code to three lines, directly lowering the risk of insecure combiner implementations. We report the first statistically rigorous per-operation overhead measurement for a Python hybrid PQC library (3,000 iterations, CPU-pinned, bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals). A full X25519 + ML-KEM-768 handshake completes in 243 μs under Docker/Linux -- 0.5--2.5% of a typical TLS 1.3 round-trip budget. At 5,000 concurrent users, throughput holds at 2,848 ops/s with only 4.9% degradation versus the single-user baseline, confirming that liboqs releases the Python GIL during C-level operations. We introduce Coefficient of Variation (CoV) as a practical timing side-channel proxy across all FIPS 203/204 operations. ML-KEM-768 decapsulation achieves CoV = 3.9%, within the AES-256-GCM noise floor (2.1%). ML-DSA-65 signing shows CoV = 51.5%, expected from FIPS 204 rejection sampling, not a side-channel. This CoV methodology has not previously been applied to PQC library evaluation and provides a lightweight complement to formal constant-time verification tools. All results are reproducible via a single Docker command.

title: Post-Quantum Discovery as a Governance Capability: Evidence-Based Cryptographic Visibility and Exposure Prioritisation in a Critical Service Provider
abs: Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC) readiness is increasingly constrained not by algorithm availability, but by cryptographic visibility, dependency complexity, and fragmented governance. This paper presents an anonymised case study of a large European critical service provider that initiated PQC readiness through a discovery first strategy, utilizing tool supported cryptographic inventorying to establish an evidence based baseline prior to migration planning. The discovery phase revealed systemic challenges, including distributed cryptographic ownership, uneven evidence quality across legacy and modern environments, and high dependency on third party cryptographic roadmaps. To operationalise these findings, the organisation introduced a structured exposure register that enabled prioritisation based on asset criticality, confidentiality longevity, and migration feasibility. We argue that PQC discovery should be understood as a governance capability that stabilises organisational knowledge and converts cryptographic uncertainty into measurable accountability, supporting risk based decision making and ecosystem coordination. The results contribute actionable lessons for institutions pursuing crypto-agility and resilience under post quantum harvest now, decrypt later threat models.

title: Quantum Futures Interactive: A Live Demonstration of Post-Quantum Blockchain Security, Infrastructure Tradeoffs, and Sustainable Distributed Trust
abs: Advances in quantum computing challenge the hardness assumptions underlying widely deployed public-key cryptography in blockchain systems. Although post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards are emerging, understanding quantum risk remains fragmented across research, engineering, governance, and investment communities. This demo presents Quantum Futures Interactive, a live interdisciplinary demonstration combining educational visualization, participatory interaction, and demonstrative post-quantum artifact generation using a toy LWE-based construction. Participants engage in a structured seven-stage interaction flow covering quantum threat education, sentiment capture, technology prioritization, infrastructure tradeoff exploration across simulators and QPUs, and artifact generation. The system integrates distributed trust concepts and sustainability-aware infrastructure considerations within an interactive decision framework.

title: MQTT Across a Raspberry Pi 5 IoT Network Utilizing Quantum-resistant Signature Algorithms
abs: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has introduced millions of resource-constrained devices into critical infrastructures, consumer environments, and industrial systems. These devices rely on lightweight communication protocols such as MQTT to support low-power, intermittent, and bandwidth-limited operation. However, common TLS algorithms used to secure MQTT communications are vulnerable to quantum attacks made feasible by Shor's algorithm. As a result, IoT infrastructures must evaluate and adopt post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) methods capable of providing long-term resilience. This report investigates the implementation of PQC algorithms within an MQTT-based IoT networks using three Raspberry Pis. Specifically, it integrates the FALCON digital signature scheme, one of NIST's selected post-quantum signature algorithms, to maintain message authenticity and integrity across resource-constrained MQTT clients and brokers. By measuring system performance, the research characterizes the practical trade-offs of deploying lattice-based PQC on lightweight hardware.

title: ORCHID: Orchestrated Reduction Consensus for Hash-based Integrity in Distributed Ledgers
abs: We present \textbf{ORCHID} (\textit{Orchestrated Reduction Consensus for Hash-based Integrity in Distributed Ledgers}), a novel bio-inspired consensus protocol that maps the neuroscientific \emph{binding problem} -- how the brain integrates distributed neural oscillations into a unified conscious percept -- onto the distributed systems \emph{consensus problem}, how blockchain nodes agree on a single ledger state under Byzantine faults. Grounded in the Penrose--Hameroff Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch~OR) hypothesis and the Kuramoto synchronisation model, ORCHID equips each node with a quantum-noisy phase oscillator; consensus is triggered when the network's order parameter $r(t)$ crosses a \emph{binding threshold} $θ_b$, mirroring the gamma-band binding event in conscious perception. ORCHID is further strengthened by a coherence-weighted Quantum Secret Sharing (QSS) layer, extending the survey framework of Weinberg to a concrete consensus application. Simulation results on Watts--Strogatz small-world networks ($n=10$--$150$) demonstrate: (i)~the Kuramoto order parameter reaches $r_{\max}=0.988$ under coupling $K=3.0$, well above the theoretical critical coupling $K_c \approx 1.41$; (ii)~a sharp QSS fidelity phase transition at coherence $c^*\approx 0.82$, confirming Theorem~2; (iii)100\% consensus rate at all tested Byzantine fractions (0\%--40\%), with median convergence under 4~s for $n=30$; and (iv)~ORCHID achieves $O(n{\cdot}k)$ message complexity, outperforming PBFT's $O(n^2)$ at $n\geq150$. These results establish ORCHID as a scalable, biologically plausible, and quantum-augmented consensus mechanism for post-quantum distributed ledgers.

title: Key Encapsulation Mechanism-Based Integrated Encryption Scheme (KEM-IES)
abs: The Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme (ECIES) is widely regarded as a practical method and has been adopted by multiple standards. However, the advancement of quantum computing technologies poses potential security risks to ECIES. Therefore, this study proposes a Key Encapsulation Mechanism-Based Integrated Encryption Scheme (KEM-IES), which enhances resistance to quantum attacks by incorporating a Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC)-based Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM). Furthermore, the study integrates the Ascon algorithm, released by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in August 2025, to further improve computational efficiency and enable applicability to embedded systems. The proposed KEM-IES and its Ascon-based variant are implemented on a Raspberry Pi 4, and evaluations are conducted to compare the performance of ECIES and KEM-IES.

title: MAGIQ: A Post-Quantum Multi-Agentic AI Governance System with Provable Security
abs: Our computing ecosystem is being transformed by two emerging paradigms: the increased deployment of agentic AI systems and advancements in quantum computing. With respect to agentic AI systems, one of the most critical problems is creating secure governing architectures that ensure agents follow their owners' communication and interaction policies and can be held accountable for the messages they exchange with other agents. With respect to quantum computing, existing systems must be retrofitted and new cryptographic mechanisms must be designed to ensure long-term security and quantum resistance. In fact, NIST recommends that standard public-key cryptographic algorithms, including RSA, Diffie-Hellman (DH), and elliptic-curve constructions (ECC), be deprecated starting in 2030 and disallowed after 2035. In this paper, we present MAGIQ, a framework for policy definition and enforcement in multi-agent AI systems using novel, highly efficient, quantum-resistant cryptographic protocols with proven security guarantees. MAGIQ (i) allows users to define rich communication and access-control policy budgets for agent-to-agent sessions and tasks, including global budgets for one-to-many agent sessions; (ii) enforces such policies using post-quantum cryptographic primitives; (iii) supports session-based enforcement of policies for agent-to-agent and one-to-many agent sessions; and (iv) provides accountability of agents to their users through message attribution. We formally model and prove the correctness and security of the system using the Universal Composability (UC) framework. We evaluate the computation and communication overhead of our framework and compare it with the state-of-the-art agentic AI framework SAGA. MAGIQ is a first step toward post-quantum-secure solutions for agentic AI systems.

title: Aquaman: A Transparent Proxy Architecture for Quantum Resilient Key Establishment
abs: The harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) threat--adversaries intercepting and archiving ciphertext today for retrospective decryption once quantum computers mature--turns the future quantum threat into a present liability for the public-key primitives (RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ECC) that anchor modern session-key exchange. We present Aquaman, a transparent-proxy architecture for quantum-resilient session-key establishment. A transparent proxy intercepts session-key requests at the edge of a trusted network without requiring client-side configuration, deploying quantum-resistant capability at the network boundary on behalf of clients that may themselves lack post-quantum cryptography (PQC). Aquaman supports four operating modes: PQC offloaded to the proxy for clients without trusted PQC stacks; classical multi-path key fragmentation over heterogeneous media (with an optional anonymous proxy-pool variant); QKD with the SKIP/ETSI GS QKD 014 key-delivery interface; and classical/PQC hybrid handshakes. We implement and evaluate the first two modes; the latter two are well-trodden in the PQC literature and we discuss but do not implement them. The implemented multi-path mode splits the session key into ciphertext fragments distributed across diverse media (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, cellular, Ethernet); reconstruction requires all fragments. We formalize the security argument and prove that recovery probability decays as (B/d)^n in the diversity dimension. A 1,000-run prototype evaluation on AWS EC2 shows that latency is dominated by network transmission, not by multi-path overhead.

title: Toward Quantum-Safe 6G: Experimental Evaluation of Post-Quantum Cryptography Techniques
abs: 6G networks will require quantum-secure cryptography deployed across core infrastructure, edge nodes, resource-constrained IoT devices. Although post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) algorithms have been standardized by NIST, their practical deployability in bandwidth and latency limited wireless systems remains unclear. This paper presents a practical evaluation of NIST selected PQC schemes, including ML-KEM (Kyber), ML-DSA (Dilithium), and Falcon.
