journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: Fault-tolerant quantum computers threaten blockchains at both the signature layer (e.g., ECDSA) and the consensus layer (e.g., Grover-accelerated hash puzzles). Most "post-quantum" proposals replace vulnerable primitives with Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC), leaving the consensus logic itself classical and quantum-accelerable. We present a quantumnative consensus protocol that uses multipartite entanglement to enforce core security properties at the level of physics. A post-quantum digital signature scheme is assumed only as a thin authentication layer for classical messages; the main logic resides in a Quantum Multi-Party Computation (QMPC) layer. Using distributed GHZ states and a sum-of-columns construction, nodes generate an information-theoretically secure random beacon and deterministically elect a round leader, after passing disturbance checks that detect tampering with high confidence. The beacon supports a standard BFT-style commit phase, yielding agreement, validity, and termination against a Quantum Polynomial Time (QPT) adversary corrupting fewer than one-third of the nodes. Quantum-circuit simulations of intercept-resend attacks validate the disturbance-detection mechanism and corroborate our theoretical analysis.

title: Obfuscated Quantum and Post-Quantum Cryptography
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: In this work, we present an experimental deployment of a new design for combined quantum key distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC). Novel to our system is the dynamic obfuscation of the QKD-PQC sequence of operations, the number of operations, and parameters related to the operations; coupled to the integration of a GPS-free quantum synchronization protocol within the QKD process. We compare the performance and overhead of our QKD-PQC system relative to a standard QKD system with one-time pad encryption, demonstrating that our design can operate in real time with little additional overhead caused by the new security features. Since our system can offer additional defensive strategies against a wide spectrum of practical attacks that undermine deployed QKD, PQC, and certain combinations of these two primitives, we suggest that our design represents one of the most secure communication systems currently available. Given the dynamic nature of its obfuscation attributes, our new system can also be adapted in the field to defeat yet-to-be-discovered practical attacks.

title: Quantum Technology Readiness Adoption Model: A TOE-Aligned Framework for Addressing Quantum Technology Risk Exposure
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: Quantum computing, quantum communication and networking, quantum sensing, and post-quantum cryptography (PQC) each require distinct organizational readiness assessment. Existing maturity models address these domains in isolation, conflate PQC with quantum technologies, omit quantum networking, exhibit regional standards bias, or mandate specific vendor relationships. The Quantum Technology Readiness Adoption Model (QTRAM), grounded in the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, structures assessment through five independent Technology sub-dimensions within shared Organization and Environment contexts, using six maturity levels (05) aligned with international standards from IEEE, NIST, ETSI, ITU, TNO, and regional bodies. QTRAM remains theoretical and requires empirical validation.

title: Toward Quantum-Resilient Software Supply Chains: A DevSecOps Case Study with Hybrid Post-Quantum Artifact Signing
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: Software supply-chain security has become a central concern due to the pervasive reuse of third-party dependencies, automated CI/CD pipelines, and the increasing number of attacks targeting build systems and artifact distribution channels. In parallel, emerging quantum computing capabilities threaten the long-term security of widely deployed public-key signatures (e.g., RSA/ECDSA) used to establish artifact authenticity. This paper reports a practitioner-led case study of a GitLab CI/CD pipeline that operationalizes DevSecOps with Shift-Left controls across linting, software composition analysis (SCA), dynamic application security testing (DAST), centralized quality governance, security orchestration, artifact packaging, and a hybrid signing workflow combining a classical Vault Transit signature and a post-quantum signature (CRYSTALS-Dilithium). The pipeline culminates in a signed bundle published to a secure store, enabling verifiable integrity under both classical and post-quantum verification regimes. The case study demonstrates how a future-resilient supply chain can be incrementally adopted without breaking existing verification flows while increasing early detection capability and improving traceability and auditability.

title: PQC-Enhanced QKD Networks: A Layered Approach
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: We present a layered and modular network architecture that combines Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) to provide scalable end-to-end security across long distance multi-hop, trusted-node quantum networks. To ensure interoperability and efficient practical deployment, hop-wise tunnels between physically secured nodes are protected by WireGuard with periodically rotated pre-shared keys sourced via the ETSI GS QKD 014 interface. On top, Rosenpass performs a PQC key exchange to establish an end-to-end data channel without modifying deployed QKD devices or network protocols. This dual-layer composition yields post-quantum forward secrecy and authenticity under practical assumptions. We implement the design using open-source components and validate and evaluate it in simulated and lab test-beds. Experiments show uninterrupted operation over multihop paths, low resource footprint and fail-safe mechanisms. We further discuss the design's compositional security, wherein the security of each individual component is preserved under their combination and outline migration paths for operators integrating QKD-aware overlays in existing infrastructures.

title: Hybrid Quantum-Secure LEO Satellite Networks
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: The quantum era compromises current cryptography, motivating the development of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) as complementary approaches to secure long-term communications. Satellite platforms are expected to extend QKD beyond terrestrial distance limits, yet their integration into broader network infrastructures introduces significant architectural and operational challenges. This work examines these challenges from a networking perspective and explores how PQC can assist early satellite-based QKD deployments. We introduce a control-plane model that combines satellite QKD for Earth-to-space key establishment with PQC-secured inter-satellite communication, enabling key delivery between ground stations when quantum keys are not yet available network-wide. A case study based on emulated keyexchange procedures using timing data derived from the Iridium constellation illustrates the feasibility of the approach.

title: Efficient Quantum Generic Key-Recovery Attack on Feistel Ciphers
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: The development of post-quantum cryptography requires cryptographic primitives that remain secure against quantum adversaries. Quantum key-recovery attacks constitute a fundamental class of quantum cryptanalytic techniques, and the resistance of a cryptosystem to such attacks serves as an important indicator of its overall security. Since the Feistel structure is a core component in the design of many block ciphers, efficient quantum key-recovery attacks on Feistel ciphers provide valuable insights into evaluating and strengthening their security. In this paper, we propose an efficient generic quantum key-recovery attack on Feistel ciphers. Our attack integrates universal hash families with Simon's and Grover's algorithms to perform key-recovery. We rigorously analyze the correctness of the proposed attack and derive its time and quantum resource complexities. A comprehensive comparison with existing keyrecovery attacks shows that the proposed approach improves both quantum resource usage and dominant query complexity, and therefore yields a more efficient quantum key-recovery attack. Our work enhances the understanding of Feistel ciphers under quantum threats and informs the design of robust cryptosystems for the post-quantum era.

title: End-to-End Adaptive Quantum-Safe Key Management in Distributed Multi-Technology 5G Architectures
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: The deployment of 5G networks has reached a high maturity level, but the complexity and heterogeneity of their architectures hinder management and protection. The emergence of quantum computing and communications raises security concerns, motivating the adoption of information-theoretic security (ITS). Integrating technologies such as Quantum-Key Distribution (QKD) and Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), often leveraging QKD-generated keys in physical- or link-layer encryption mechanisms, is a key research direction. However, the distributed complexity of 5G, together with the practical challenges of QKD, makes full QKD integration difficult. It is therefore necessary to develop a high-level system to manage security in 5G deployments where QKD and classical capabilities coexist. This paper presents an end-to-end (E2E) adaptive quantum-safe key management system based on a centralized controller. Using a hybrid approach (QKD and PQC), we define multiple Security Levels depending on the quantum-awareness of network nodes in the E2E path, orchestrating key establishment from the centralized Quantum Security Controller (QuSeC). The proposed framework has been implemented in a multi-site 5G network using free5GC and UERANSIM, together with commercial QKD equipment from LuxQuanta and Quantum Optics Jena, with framework-provided keys securing different inter-site 5G interfaces. Results show that integrating the adaptive framework for E2E key establishment in distributed 5G networks introduces a one-time latency in the initial handshake, depending on the underlying quantum infrastructure, while subsequent processes remain comparable and can even reduce overhead, demonstrating that stronger quantum-safe security can be achieved without significantly impacting performance.

title: Implementation of a Hybrid QKD/PQC Network and Applications
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: The European Quantum Communication Infrastructure (EuroQCI) initiative is fostering the deployment of national quantum key distribution (QKD) testbeds across the European Union. In this context, we report on the design, implementation, and evaluation of the Austrian testbed, with a particular focus on advances in key management and applicationlevel integration of QKD. First, we introduce a hybrid key management system (KMS) that combines QKD-derived keys in a decentralized architecture with post-quantum authenticated key exchange, enabling end-to-end hybrid keys while reducing trust assumptions in intermediate nodes. Second, we present three QKD-enabled applications: (i) a secure secret-sharing-based storage system leveraging QKD-protected share distribution, (ii) a QKD-integrated extension of Jitsi employing ETSI GS QKD 014 group keys to reduce overhead in multi-party communication, and (iii) a hybrid QKD/PQC WireGuard-based VPN enabling QKD-secured HSM backup operations without requiring modifications to proprietary HSM protocols. Finally, we describe the deployment of these solutions in a national network comprising a four-node metropolitan testbed and a 200 km long-distance link with trusted nodes, and provide performance measurements for both the network and the hybrid KMS. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating QKD into heterogeneous applications and hybrid cryptographic infrastructures.

title: Combined Quantum and Post-Quantum Security Performance Under Finite Keys
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: Recent advances in quantum-secure communication have highlighted the value of hybrid schemes that combine Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) with Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). Yet most existing hybrid designs omit realistic finite-key effects on QKD key rates and do not specify how to maintain security when both QKD and PQC primitives leak information through side-channels. These gaps limit the applicability of hybrid systems in practical, deployed networks. In this work, we advance a recently proposed hybrid QKD-PQC system by integrating tight finite-key security to the QKD primitive and improving the design for better scalability. This hybrid system employs an information-theoretically secure instruction sequence that determines the configurations of different primitives and thus ensures message confidentiality even when both the QKD and the PQC primitives are compromised. The novelty in our work lies in the implementation of the tightest finite-key security to date for the BBM92 protocol and the design improvements in the primitives of the hybrid system that ensure the processing time scales linearly with the size of secret instructions.

title: SQUIRE - A Global Quantum Resistant Communication Service for IoT
journal: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC)
abs: Asymmetric cryptographic algorithms commonly used in Internet of Things (IoT) systems — such as Rivest─Shamir─Adleman (RSA) and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) - are vulnerable to quantum attacks, posing a risk to the long-term security of devices and data. This work presents SQUIRE (Secure Quantum-Integrated Resilience for Embedded Systems), a lightweight and scalable communication framework designed for quantum-resistant IoT systems. SQUIRE integrates validated quantum randomness with classical and post-quantum cryptographic techniques to enable secure key exchange that is resilient against both classical and quantum adversaries. By leveraging Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs) and existing communication infrastructure, SQUIRE provides seamless end-to-end security without requiring specialized quantum communication hardware, making it practical for a wide range of IoT environments, from smart homes to industrial systems.

title: Beyond the Quantum Horizon: Balancing Post-Quantum Security and Real-Time Performance in UAVs
journal: International Conference on Pattern Analysis and Intelligent Systems (PAIS)
abs: The advent of Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers (FTQC), or Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQC), is radically redefining the security paradigm for Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS). While current communication protocols, such as secure MAVLink, rely on cryptographic foundations deemed robust against classical computation, the application of specific quantum algorithms threatens to render these protections obsolete. This paper examines attack vectors targeting Command and Control (C2) links and telemetry, while highlighting the urgent need for a transition toward Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) standards tailored to the hardware constraints of drones. The implementation of PQC on resource-constrained architectures, such as the ARM Cortex-M4 core, imposes critical performance requirements. For a UAV, the latency induced by cryptographic primitives can compromise the real-time attitude control loop. Thus, the transition from ECDH to the ML-KEM (Kyber) standard represents a significant optimization challenge, where post-quantum security must be balanced against raw algorithmic efficiency to ensure system survival and operational integrity.

title: Authentication Mechanisms in ARM Architecture Devices
journal: International Conference on Pattern Analysis and Intelligent Systems (PAIS)
abs: The ARM architecture dominates IoT, healthcare, and embedded systems, ranging from ultra-low-power CortexM microcontrollers to high-performance Cortex-A processors. Providing secure authentication on these devices is challenging because cryptographic operations must satisfy stringent energy, memory, and latency constraints. Classical mechanisms, particularly optimized elliptic-curve cryptography, offer strong security with moderate cost, while lightweight authenticated ciphers enable sub-millisecond authentication for continuous sensing applications. However, emerging quantum threats jeopardize the longterm security of classical solutions. Recent studies have therefore evaluated post-quantum schemes such as Kyber, Saber, and Dilithium on ARM platforms, demonstrating practical feasibility through DSP extensions, memory-efficient implementations, and parameter tuning. Hybrid classical-post-quantum constructions further provide transitional security with manageable overhead. This survey presents a systematic review of authentication mechanisms on ARM-based devices and introduces a unified taxonomy and quantitative comparison framework. Execution time, energy consumption, memory footprint, and security guarantees are analyzed with emphasis on resource-constrained healthcare IoT, highlighting key trade-offs.

title: Quantum Key Distribution in the Post-Quantum Era: Technologies and Deployment Perspectives
abs: Quantum computing advances pose a serious threat to conventional public-key cryptographic systems such as RSA and elliptic curve cryptography as quantum algorithms may undermine the computational assumptions that guaranty their security. This challenge has driven the development of quantumsafe security approaches among which Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) represents a fundamentally different paradigm based on quantum mechanical principles rather than mathematical complexity. This paper presents a structured review of recent progress in QKD based on a systematic analysis of literature between 2020 and 2025, we examine core protocols including discrete-variable, continuous-variable, measurement-deviceindependent, and twin-field approaches, while also discussing their relationship with post-quantum cryptography as a complementary strategy for future secure communication systems. We provide a unified comparison framework to support practical design and policy decisions by organizing protocols and implementations along deployment dimensions. The study analyze theoretical foundations, implementation technologies across fiber, free-space, satellite, and integrated photonic platforms, and key performance trade-offs involving scalability, security robustness, and deployment feasibility. Findings indicate substantial progress in transitioning QKD from laboratory research toward practical implementations, supported by advances in network architectures, integrated hardware and hybrid cryptographic designs. The comparative analysis will highlight distinct strengths and limitations among protocol families and emphasize the potential of combining QKD with post-quantum cryptographic methods to enhance resilience. Remaining challenges including scalability constraints, implementation-level vulnerabilities, performance limitations over long distances, and integration with existing communication infrastructures are critically discussed. Finally, emerging research directions such as quantum repeaters, hybrid quantum-classical security models, and exploratory directions such as artificial intelligence-assisted optimizations are identified as key factors in enabling the evolution of QKD toward largescale quantum-secure networking.

title: Quantum Vault X
journal: International Conference on Trends in Material Science and Inventive Materials (ICTMIM)
abs: As digital threats continuously evolve at a rapid pace, and as quantum computing is likely to affect classical cryptographic systems, the current security measures are becoming inefficient in safeguarding sensitive digital data. The paper describes Quantum Vault X, a secure file storage system that has been developed based on post-quantum cryptography schemes and a layered authentication system to provide long term confidentiality and integrity of stored data. The suggested system is designed to apply a zeroknowledge client controlled security design where the plaintext data and the encryption keys will be inaccessible to the storage provider. Quantum Vault X combines multi-factor authentication with biometric verification (fingerprint/facial recognition), voice-based authentication and a client-side cryptography secret encrypted by memory-hard password hashing. The postquantum security is accomplished by encapsulating key encryption with the help of the CRYSTALS-Kyber which allows the key encryption to be secured with quantum resistance. Each user file is ensured with AES256 encryption at the client, the encryption keys are encapsulated and then stored, ensuring that failure to access the server does not succeed in decryption and storage of the data. The proposed system incorporates the elements of the post-quantum cryptography, zeroknowledge principles, and multi-modal authentication, which proves a robust and viable security framework to counter the existing and emerging cyber threats.

title: Quantum-Resistant Certificateless Lattice-Based Signature Scheme for IoT Security
journal: International Conference on Trends in Material Science and Inventive Materials (ICTMIM)
abs: The rapid proliferation of IoT technology has brought billions of devices into play that need to operate in a variety of diverse, resource-constrained environments. Secure authentication among these devices is a critical challenge, as traditional certificate-based public key infrastructures incur heavy computation and management overhead. Moreover, recent breakthroughs in quantum computing put at risk the security of classical cryptographic algorithms commonly used in IoT systems. This paper proposes a post-quantum certificateless authentication framework designed to address the efficiency-long-term security requirements of IoT environments. The proposed framework uses lattice-based cryptography to resist quantum-enabled adversaries while eliminating the need for digital certificates. The certificateless approach evades the problem of key escrow of identity-based cryptography and simplifies the key management process. A lightweight authentication protocol, which is suitable for constrained IoT devices, is developed. Security analyses prove that our proposed framework resists common attacks such as impersonation, replay, and man-in-the-middle attacks. The performance evaluation shows that our proposed framework reduces the communication and computational overheads compared with the traditional certificatebased authentication schemes. In this way, it is appropriate for large-scale and futureproof deployments of IoT systems.

title: Quantum Safe Vehicle Networks Using ML and IoT for Traffic Congestion Prediction
journal: International Conference on Trends in Material Science and Inventive Materials (ICTMIM)
abs: The rapid growth of connected and autonomous vehicles has accelerated the adoption of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), enabling real-time communication among vehicles, roadside units, and cloud services to support intelligent traffic management and road safety. However, the increasing dependence on wireless communication introduces significant security challenges, which are expected to intensify with the advancement of quantum computing that threatens conventional cryptographic methods. To address these concerns, this paper presents a quantum-safe IoV framework that integrates post-quantum cryptography concepts with machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. The framework is designed to support quantumresistant security mechanisms for future vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication while maintaining data integrity and privacy. In addition, an ML-based traffic congestion prediction approach is utilized to analyze vehicular and sensor data for intelligent traffic management. The system was evaluated using 15,200 vehicular records collected from 92 vehicles over a 30 day period. The congestion prediction model achieved an accuracy of 94.6%, with precision and recall values of 92.8% and 93.4%, respectively. A nearby vehicle approaching alert mechanism is implemented using an ESP32-based hardware prototype to enhance driver awareness through dashboard visualization. The alert subsystem demonstrated a detection accuracy of 95.2% with an average response time of 120 ms. Furthermore, edge-level deployment reduced processing latency to 87 ms compared to 305 ms in a cloud-only configuration. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating secure communication frameworks with intelligent traffic prediction and real-time alerts in IoV environments, highlighting the potential of the proposed approach for next-generation intelligent transportation systems.

title: HIRZ: Hybrid Post-Quantum Cryptography for Secure Long-Term Data Archiving
abs: Organizations managing long-term archives face harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks, where adversaries collect encrypted data today for future quantum decryption. While NIST has standardized post-quantum algorithms (CRYSTALS-Kyber, CRYSTALS-Dilithium), pure post-quantum deployment faces regulatory and infrastructure barriers. This paper presents Hirz, a hybrid cryptographic system combining ECDH-secp384r1 with Kyber-1024 and Dilithium5 for archival workloads requiring 20─30 year confidentiality. Our implementation using OpenSSL 3.2.0 and liboqs 0.10.1 achieves 18% overhead compared to classical systems (29.7 ms versus 25.2 ms for 100 MB files) on commodity Intel hardware. Comparative evaluation demonstrates that hybrid construction adds only 11% overhead versus pure post-quantum while providing regulatory compliance, backward compatibility, and defense against algorithm vulnerabilities. The system incorporates threat-driven 12 month key rotation, dual-signature verification, and X.509v3 PKI extensions supporting 30 year certificate chains.

title: Accelerating Post-Quantum Cryptography via LLM-Driven Hardware-Software Co-Design
journal: 2026 27th International Symposium on Quality Electronic Design (ISQED)
abs: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is crucial for securing data against emerging quantum threats. However, its algorithms are computationally complex and difficult to implement efficiently on hardware. In this paper, we explore the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) to accelerate the hardware-software co-design process for PQC, with a focus on the FALCON digital signature scheme. We present a novel framework that leverages LLMs to analyze PQC algorithms, identify performance-critical components, and generate candidate hardware descriptions for FPGA implementation. We present the first quantitative comparison between LLM-driven synthesis and conventional HLS-based approaches for low-level compute-intensive kernels in FALCON, showing that human-in-the-loop LLM-generated accelerators can achieve up to$2.6 \times$speedup in kernel execution time with shorter critical paths, while highlighting trade-offs in resource utilization and power consumption. Our results suggest that LLMs can minimize design effort and development time by automating FPGA accelerator design iterations for PQC algorithms, offering a promising new direction for rapid and adaptive PQC accelerator design on FPGAs.

title: Blockchain-Based Digital Content Integrity Systems: A Comprehensive Review of Multi-Layered Security Approaches and Tamper Detection Mechanisms
journal: 2026 IEEE 16th Symposium on Computer Applications & Industrial Electronics (ISCAIE)
abs: We provide a comprehensive review of blockchain technology applications, challenges, and trends facing the field of digital security and data integrity verification. We perform a systematic review of over 60 peer-reviewed papers written between 2008 and 2024 and classify blockchain applications in the following four key domains: Digital Content Integrity, Identity Management & Authentication, Secure Data Storage & Sharing, and Network Security & Intrusion Detection. Following our analysis conclusions, we reasoned that under controlled conditions, blockchain-based systems perform approximately 89%-100% accuracy in applications with multiple security objectives, but these systems had difficulties in scaling, processing overhead$(\text{5 0 ~ m s}-\text{2 5 0 0 ~ m s})$, energy consumption, and interoperability across platforms. We emphasize the significant gaps in our research, including quantum-resistant cryptography, real-time processing capabilities, privacy-preserving mechanisms, and universal format-agnostic solutions. We also provide a multi-level reference framework, which we propose to guide and inform system design in the future versus assuming readiness for deployment. This framework is used as a conceptual example for this architecture; the experimental demonstration is provided in the appendix. The experimental results are not intended to provide a benchmark comparison or an in-depth analysis of the current state quo but as a demonstration of the framework's promise in context. We provide future research directions for the incorporation of post-quantum cryptography, federated learning, optimization of edge computing, and standardized cross-chain protocols. This review serves as a foundational source for academics, practitioners, and policymakers in blockchain security, digital forensics, cybersecurity, and integrity verification.

title: Magnetic Vortex Nanodisk Arrays as Physical Unclonable Functions
journal: 2026 IEEE International Magnetic Conference - Short Papers (INTERMAG Short Papers)
abs: Quantum computing threatens conventional cryptography, necessitating physically-grounded security primitives. We present magnetic vortex nanodisk arrays as high-entropy Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs). Each nanodisk encodes binary chirality and polarity states via Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert dynamics, providing 2 N entropy bits for N disks. Substrate defects deterministically modulate spin wave propagation for device-bound encryption. The framework exhibits modeling resistance through nonlinear dynamics, cloning resistance via atomic-scale variations, and quantum resistance through absence of algorithmic structure, yielding practical post-quantum cryptographic primitives.

title: Hybrid Cryptography Approaches for Securing Data Transmission in Wireless Body Sensor Networks
journal: 2026 International Conference on Multidisciplinary Innovations For Smart & Sustainable Future (MISSF)
abs: The Wireless Body Sensor Networks (WBSNs) require security measures, which are capable of resisting the ever-changing cyber-threats without violating the tight computational and energy limits. The conventional hybrid cryptography products are based on the combination of fixed symmetric primitives and asymmetric primitives, which can cast some vulnerabilities to key-predictability, small entropy, and even increasing post-quantum threats. To overcome these drawbacks, this paper presents a new security architecture nicknamed Adaptive Multiphase Cryptographic Fusion (AMCF) which is aimed at fostering a dynamically fashioned cryptography landscape that is optimal towards wearable physiological sensing systems. AMCF combines three fundamental innovations: Physiological micro-variation and chaotic micro-reactor combining physiological micro-variation and chaotic dynamics to produce per-segment ephemeral keys; Multiphase Encryption Core for switching between various encryption "phases" from a lightweight symmetric cryptography to hybrid elliptic curve encryption (HEC) and finally to quantum resilient lattice-based encryption; Micro-Segment Transport Encoder to chop up the transmissions into independently encrypted pieces called "micro-units" to avoid interception and reconstructing under interception. A decisionmaking system that is sensitive to energy is used to select a phase that enables a robust security but does not impact the battery life. Cooperation of adaptive cryptographic depth, physiological entropy harvesting and probabilistic engagement of postquantum components in AMCF, improves significantly confidentiality and resistance to interception, spoofing, and future cryptographic attacks. The suggested approach lays the groundwork of safe, scalable, and energy-congruous information security in wearable healthcare systems of the next generation. The proposed AMCF technique attained an overall accuracy of 97.4%.

title: Post-Quantum Secure Mail with Forward Secrecy and Zero-Knowledge Architecture
journal: International Conference on Innovations in Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Development (ICIETSD)
abs: In this paper, we propose our secure cloud-based mail ands messaging system Mail which uses a combination of hybrid post-quantum-cryptography (PQC) and classical elliptic-curve communication scheme in order to ensure long-term confidentiality as well as forward secrecy. The construction is based on X25519 and Kyber-768 in the form of hybrid key exchange, Ed25519 as digital signature, and ChaCha20-Poly1305 for authenticated encryption. For increased message confidentiality and post-compromise security, we employ a Double Ratchet mechanism inspired by the Signal protocol in conjunction with JWT authentication and MAC-level integrity protection. The prototype is implemented on the server side using a Flask (python) implementation with PostgreSQL as persistence similar to 38 and WatIO. React client handling the encryption, side key client. Experimental tests demonstrate that such a design effectively combines practical deployability and strong cryptographic security guarantees against classical, as well as quantum adversaries. This work attempts to bridge the gap between research-related PQC models and practical secure communication systems.

title: Quantum-Safe Neuro-Symbolic Intelligence: A Lossless Framework for Vertical Federated Learning in Decoupled Data Silos
journal: 2026 Third International Conference on Networking and Communications (ICNWC)
abs: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as an effective paradigm for collaborative model development in privacy-sensitive domains such as healthcare and finance. While FL avoids direct data sharing, existing frameworks struggle to simultaneously support rich feature representation, high predictive accuracy, and durable cryptographic security. Practically, numerous privacy protection measures culminate into observable performance degradation and the rapidly growing pace of quantum computing seriously draws questions on the reliability of classical encryption protocols in the long-run. To overcome these issues this paper proposes Quantum-Safe Neuro-Symbolic Intelligence (QS-NSI), a hybrid model that will be used in Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) across decoupled data silos. The suggested architecture integrates deep neural networks with robust feature representation with the decision trees based on SecureBoost to have interpretability, as well as lossless predictive power. Moreover, lattice-based post-quantum cryptographic methods are implemented to protect federated communication against quantum-enabled attacks without causing a lot of added computational burden. Empirical results indicate that the proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 99.14%, closely aligning with centralized learning performance while preserving strict privacy constraints. By effectively balancing privacy, accuracy, and security, QS-NSI offers a scalable, interpretable, and quantum-resilient solution for next-generation distributed intelligence systems.

title: Advancing ATM through Info centric and Composable Service Architectures
abs: Current Air Traffic Management (ATM) systems for enroute and Terminal Maneuvering Area (TMA) operations are monolithic, vendor-specific, and built on proprietary middleware, limiting scalability, innovation, and cost-efficiency. In Europe, 80% of the Air Navigation Service Providers (ANSPs) consider their current architecture not-fit-for-purpose, when asked about the readiness to cope with future challenges such as increased traffic growth or rising cybersecurity and resilience demands. Today, expectations have evolved toward service-oriented architectures, emphasizing interoperability, portability, and service interchangeability. The currently ongoing global ATM modernization is increasingly defined by the transition to info centric, service oriented, cloud native architectures. Both the U.S. Info centric NAS framework and the European New Service Delivery Model (NSDM) emphasize standardized information models, decoupled functional services, and dynamic composability across distributed, safety critical environments. These developments mark a shift from monolithic, tightly coupled ATM systems to federated, high assurance, microservice based ecosystems capable of supporting evolving operational concepts.Next generation platforms leverage containerized microservices orchestrated via control planes to deploy operational functions with fine grained scalability and fault isolation. Core components include 4D trajectory management services, deterministic real time data distribution backbones implementing publish/subscribe and request/response interaction patterns, and AI augmented automation modules constrained by safety oriented training data. High integrity performance is achieved through time bounded message sequencing, state synchronization protocols, and consistency preserving replication strategies that maintain a unified airspace picture across ANSP boundaries. Concepts such as Zero-Trust Architecture, Defense in Depth, and Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) are becoming essential, influencing system design at the core level.Support for Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) is realized through standardized trajectory schemas aligned with FIXM/FF ICE, continuous 4D trajectory updates, and cross domain sharing over SWIM compliant interfaces. Cloud native execution environments utilize service meshes, zero trust security patterns, latency-, jitter-, and packet loss monitoring in real time. Elastic compute scaling is driven by traffic complexity metrics and demand forecasting models, ensuring deterministic system behavior under variable load conditions.Next generation digital platforms will consolidate surveillance/automation modules, runway/approach optimization services, voice communication services (VCS), among others within a unified microservice architecture. Such platforms apply composable service constructs (CSC). These include standardized API contracts, container based deployment units, and identity aware authorization policies to integrate multi vendor components without compromising certification pathways. Continuous Verification and Validation (V&V) processes use automated regression testing, static/dynamic code analysis, container attestation, and safety constraint enforcement within continuous integration / continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines adapted for safety critical domains.Cybersecurity and safety assurance are implemented through runtime service isolation, hardware rooted trust anchors, cryptographic domain segmentation, and cross domain guards to enforce controlled information exchange. Integrated monitoring frameworks employ anomaly detection ML models to identify deviations in controller interactions, trajectory states, or network behavior. Alignment with the European ATM Master Plan supports capabilities such as dynamic airspace configuration, multi node decision support orchestration, and standardized air ground communication services.The adoption of composability as a foundational engineering principle enables rapid integration of advanced operational capabilities including digital/remote tower services, AI supported conflict detection and resolution, AMAN/DMAN sequencing, and cloud based separation assurance functions. Modular architectures reduce functional coupling, support container level failover, and ensure deterministic fail safe operation under partial degradation scenarios. Multi cloud and hybrid deployments provide geographic redundancy, latency optimized routing, and cross regional federation of ATS services.The shift toward info centric, cloud native, and composable service architectures establishes a robust technical foundation for global ATM modernization. Through standardized data models, microservice orchestration, SWIM based interoperability, and AI enhanced automation, future ATM systems achieve deterministic performance, enhanced resilience, and scalable cross border operations. These architectures form a harmonized blueprint for modernization, delivering measurable improvements in safety, efficiency, and environmental performance.

title: Evaluating the Quantum Capabilities in Factorization RSA Modulus
journal: International Conference on Frontiers of Engineering and Emerging Technologies (FET)
abs: Quantum computing has emerged as a groundbreaking technology, revolutionizing the speed and capabilities of computation. Traditional computing, based on bits represented by 0s and 1s, has limitations in storage and computational efficiency, even with parallel processing. In contrast, quantum computing operates on qubits, enabling exponential reductions in storage requirements and faster computation via quantum parallelism. One prominent quantum algorithm, Shor's Algorithm, presents a significant threat to RSA encryption. This Algorithm efficiently factors large integers, a task considered intractable for classical computers. By leveraging classical and quantum computation techniques, Shor's Algorithm employs the Euclidean algorithm and the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) to find the greatest common divisor and perform period-finding, respectively. This research paper explores the implementation and implications of Shor's Algorithm in breaking RSA encryption. Through experiments conducted in IBM's Quantum Lab, the Algorithm successfully factorizes integers, showcasing its efficacy in practice. By examining the potential impact of quantum computing on RSA and exploring the capabilities of Shor's Algorithm, this research contributes to advancing the field of quantum computing and understanding its implications for modern cryptographic systems. The findings underscore the need for post-quantum cryptography to ensure secure communication and data protection in the era of quantum computing.

title: Reducing Post-Quantum Cryptography Overhead in IoT Networks Using an Epoch-Based Compression Approach
journal: International Conference on Frontiers of Engineering and Emerging Technologies (FET)
abs: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) protects against future quantum attacks but introduces significant bandwidth overhead for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices. This paper presents an epoch-based architecture combining LZ4 compression with ML-KEM-512 key encapsulation to reduce transmission costs in bandwidth-limited IoT networks. Hardware benchmarks on ESP32-DevKitC demonstrate that ML-KEM-512 key operations complete in under 20 ms total, with LZ4 compression achieving 1.04─2.34× ratios on realistic IoT payloads in under 0.5 ms. At N=100 messages per epoch, the PQC bandwidth gap relative to compressed classical ECDH narrows from 478% down to 8.3%, and the amortized ML-KEM-512 overhead reduces to 15.68 bytes per message. Although the absolute PQC penalty remains a fixed 1,440 bytes per epoch when comparing equal compression baselines, session batching makes this overhead practically negligible. A device tier taxonomy maps RFC 7228 device classes to PQC capability requirements. The results indicate that compression-assisted PQC is viable for IoT deployments where message batching is feasible.

title: Assessing Quantum Decryption Risks to Indonesian National Cryptographic Infrastructure Through Systematic Review and Mathematical Risk Modeling
journal: International Conference on Frontiers of Engineering and Emerging Technologies (FET)
abs: The extensive integration of Elliptic Curve Cryptography within Indonesia's Critical Information Infrastructure presents a severe security paradox. While these cryptographic primitives currently facilitate efficient digital transactions for the Digital Population Identity and the national payment gateway, their reliance on the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem renders them fundamentally vulnerable to polynomial time attacks via Shor's algorithm on Fault Tolerant Quantum Computers. This study provides a comprehensive quantitative risk assessment by synthesizing the 2024 to 2025 regulatory landscape with mathematical risk modeling. Utilizing Mosca's Inequality and the proposed Quantum Adjusted Risk Score, we demonstrate that the Harvest Now Decrypt Later threat profile for Indonesia is at a critical level. Our results indicate a Quantum Deficit of approximately 22 years for national health data, meaning the migration window combined with the data shelf life significantly exceeds the estimated time to quantum supremacy. This paper recommends an immediate transition to hybrid cryptographic schemes and the enforcing of crypto agility mandates across all strategic sectors.

title: Technical Gap Analysis and Policy Evaluation of SSL & TLS Security within the National Vital Information Infrastructure
journal: International Conference on Frontiers of Engineering and Emerging Technologies (FET)
abs: In the era of digital transformation, the security of National Vital Information Infrastructure (IIVN) is the main foundation of national resilience. The Secure Socket Layer/Transport Layer Security (SSL/TLS) protocol is a key pillar in ensuring the confidentiality and integrity of data in transit. However, technical implementation in the field is often not in line with established cybersecurity policies. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of SSL/TLS security in the NIVI sector in Indonesia through an evaluative approach without physical support tools. The methodology used is a gap analysis that compares actual configuration standards with national regulations (Presidential Regulation 82/2022) and the international standard NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2. The results of the analysis show that there are significant risks due to the use of deprecated protocol versions (TLS 1.0/1.1) and weak cipher suites in several strategic sectors. The gap analysis reveals that while TLS 1.2 is widely adopted, a significant portion of government and health sectors (approximately 35%) still rely on deprecated TLS 1.0/1.1 protocols. This technical debt is compounded by a high strategic dependency, where over 80% of digital certificates are issued by foreign CAs, highlighting a critical threat to national digital sovereignty. In addition, dependence on foreign Certificate Authorities (CAs) was identified as a potential threat to national data sovereignty. This study proposes a framework for strengthening SSL/TLS, including a roadmap for migrating to TLS 1.3 and preparing for post-quantum cryptography. These findings are expected to serve as strategic recommendations for IIVN managers and the National Cyber and Crypto Agency (BSSN) in strengthening Indonesia's cyber defense.

title: Comparative Efficiency Analysis of PQC Hash Algorithms (Ascon vs. SHA-3) on 64-bit Architecture for Military Data Integrity Systems
journal: International Conference on Frontiers of Engineering and Emerging Technologies (FET)
abs: In the transformation toward the Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2) paradigm, tactical data integrity is an important part of national defense. The threat of quantum computing through Grover's algorithm makes it necessary to move quickly to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) standards. This research evaluates the performance of Ascon-Hash-256 which was the winner of the NIST LWC competition, compared to SHA3-256 on a modern 64-bit architecture (AMD Zen 4). Using a low-level benchmarking methodology with RDTSCP instructions and core isolation (taskset), this study measures Cycles per Byte (CPB) efficiency for different tactical payloads (64B to 1MB). The test results show that Ascon-Hash-256 is consistently better than SHA3-256 in all scenarios. The biggest advantage is in the telemetry payload (64 bytes) with an efficiency of 24.89 CPB, or 31.8% faster than SHA-3. Technical analysis shows that Ascon's smaller internal state (320-bit) reduces register pressure on the x86_64 architecture compared to the 1600-bit state of SHA-3. These findings confirm that Ascon has great potential for high-performance military systems that need low latency and quantum resilience according to the latest 2024 FIPS standards.

title: QSec-Trace: Hybrid Quantum Classical Integrity Verification and Provenance for Cloud Logs
journal: International Conference on Emerging Computational Intelligence (ICECI)
abs: Incident response, compliance, and digital forensics require cloud audit and platform logs which in multi-tenant cloud environments can be anti-forensically manipulated through deletion, injection, rearrangement, and time distortion. To improve chain-of-custody and offer quantum awareness of integrity, in this paper, we introduce QSec-Trace, a quantum classical framework with hybrid traces of logs and tampering detection. The strategy secures logs with post-quantum signing, Merkle-based commitments, validates batch integrity with quantum fingerprinting with SWAP-test fidelity checks, identifies behavioral deviation with Isolation Forest, and integrates evidence with Bayesian fusion to compute the likelihood of tampering in the presence of uncertainty and noise. Baselines based on hash-chain and blockchain results in experiments on realistic audit-log settings have 99.2% tamper-detection accuracy, 0.99 F1score, and 0.5% false positive. Sensitivity analysis indicates that a single-bit change in a 1000-log batch makes the average fidelity of fingerprints decrease to 0.854 instead of 1.000 and robustness gets much lower as the error rate at the gate is more than 10%. Scalability of the framework is also efficient in that 64 KB fingerprint can support batches with 50,000 log entries. Overall, QSec-Trace offers verifiable provenance binding and hybrid integrity evidence to be used in cloud logs investigations.

title: A Hybrid Image Encryption Scheme with Wavelet Transform and Chaotic Permutation For Enhanced Security
journal: International Conference on Emerging Computational Intelligence (ICECI)
abs: With the emergence of quantum computing, conventional cryptographic mechanisms are under serious threat. Therefore, there is a need to design more secure alternatives. We propose a hybrid image encryption scheme that is resistant to quantum attacks. Our design combines the Kyber512 key-encapsulation mechanism for securely exchanging keys, and Ascon-128 authenticated encryption for efficient symmetric encryption. For stronger security, we used the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to decompose the image into frequency subbands and a 4D coupled logistic map to shuffle the approximation sub-band, achieving strong, quantitatively validated diffusion and confusion properties. We analyzed the scheme using extensive security evaluations, including histogram analysis, pixel correlation, information entropy, resistance against differential attacks (NPCR and UACI), structural similarity index (SSIM), and key sensitivity tests. Experimental results show that our approach successfully randomizes pixel values, decorrelates, attains near-ideal entropy ($\approx 7.999$), demonstrates high robustness against differential (NPCR $\approx 99.6 \%$ and UACI $\approx 33.5$, statistical and brute-force attacks, maintains key sensitivity, and provides strong SSIM recovery upon decryption ($0.997$). Compared with recent methods, the proposed scheme achieves higher or competitive entropy and lower pixel correlation. Formal analysis confirms security under established cryptographic assumptions, and the overall complexity is linear (O(MN))) in terms of image size. The proposed design offers a practical and scalable solution for postquantum secure image transmission in sensitive domains, such as healthcare, defense, and surveillance.

title: A Cryptography-Driven Dual-Layer Quantum-Resilient Detection Architecture for Secure Cloud Data Access
journal: 2026 9th International Conference on Trends in Electronics and Informatics (ICOEI)
abs: Data security has become a critical challenge in cloud computing as organizations increasingly depend on cloud-based digital infrastructure for data storage, processing, and intelligent services. The expansion of cloud adoption has simultaneously intensified security threats, including unauthorized access, data manipulation, and cryptographic attacks This paper introduces a novel cryptography-driven detection framework that integrates symmetric encryption with quantum-resilient code-based cryptography to safeguard cloud data. The proposed Code-Driven Dual-Layer Quantum-Resilient Detection System (CDD-QDS) architecture employs the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) to ensure fast and reliable data confidentiality, while a McEliece-inspired code-based cryptographic layer is utilized to secure key exchange and resist post-quantum attacks. Unlike conventional security models that treat encryption and intrusion detection independently, the proposed approach embeds detection capabilities within cryptographic operations by monitoring decoding behavior, error patterns, and key entropy. This integrated strategy enables early identification of malicious activities targeting cloud infrastructure before data decryption occurs. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is validated through comparative performance analysis, focusing on data integrity preservation, confidentiality assurance, detection accuracy, and computational overhead. Experimental results demonstrate that the integrated cryptographic detection mechanism enhances cloud security by 98.7% accuracy and 0.8% FPR while maintaining efficiency in machine-learning-based cloud environments.

title: Deep Neural IC Architecture Inspired by the IBM Watson Chip for Federated and Blockchain-Enabled Predictive Disease Diagnosis
journal: 2026 International Conference on AI-Driven Innovations & Applications (IC-AIDA)
abs: Modern healthcare diagnostics are challenged by fragmented patient data, stringent privacy laws (HIPAA, GDPR), and high-latency AI processing across distributed sources [1] [2]. We propose a novel cognitive AI framework that integrates IBM Watson neurosilicon hardware with federated learning, blockchain security, and quantum- inspired optimization for end-to-end predictive diagnosis. At the hardware layer, Watson's neuromorphic chipset performs low-latency inference on multimodal medical sensor inputs (e.g., ECG, MRI, genomics) with on-chip DNN acceleration [3]. The software stack uses TensorFlow Federated (TFF) to train a global model across hospital nodes, sharing only encrypted model updates. Gradients and patient records are verified via Hyperledger Fabric smart contracts, ensuring tamper-proof audit trails [4] [5]. A Quantum layer (IBM Qiskit) performs periodic hyperparameter optimization and quantum-safe key generation. This "Quantum-Federated Optimization" (QFO) strategy reduces model convergence time by $\boldsymbol{\sim} \mathbf{4 5 \%}$. In simulation with MIMIC-IV and other clinical datasets, our system achieved a $7.6 \times$ faster diagnostic inference rate than CPU baselines, 98.3% prediction accuracy, and 100% immutable record integrity (no fraud/integrity breach detected). The integrated stack includes Watson APIs, TFF, Hyperledger Fabric, and Qiskit on Python 3.11.

title: Diagnostic Case Study: Client-Side and Ecosystem Barriers in Integrating Post-Quantum Cryptography Kyber768 Into TLS 1.3
journal: 2026 International Conference on Current Research in Artificial Intelligence and Data Science (ICCRAIDS)
abs: The advancement of quantum computing poses a significant threat to widely deployed public-key cryptographic algorithms. In response, post-quantum cryptography (PQC) integration within Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 is recommended as a transitional strategy. This paper presents a diagnostic case study analyzing the real-world deployment barriers of integrating the CRYSTALS-Kyber768 key encapsulation mechanism into TLS 1.3. An experimental cloud-based server was explicitly configured using OpenSSL 3.2.3 and the Open Quantum Safe (OQS) Provider to support a hybrid X25519+Kyber768 key exchange. However, empirical observations revealed that the negotiated TLS handshake consistently fell back to classical elliptic-curve cryptography (X25519). Through detailed diagnostic analysis, this study identifies two primary ecosystem barriers: the lack of client-side capability to advertise Kyber-supported groups in the ClientHello message, and intermediary infrastructure (e.g., CDNs) terminating connections with classical ECDSA certificates. Rather than presenting a failed deployment, this research highlights critical gaps between PQC standardization and practical adoption, emphasizing that server-side readiness is insufficient without a synchronized, end-to-end ecosystem upgrade.

title: Q-Learning-Enhanced GANs for Secure 5G Access Control: Integrating Adaptive Policy Enforcement and Cryptographic Authorization
journal: International Conference on Electronic Engineering and Information Systems (EEISS)
abs: The fifth-generation (5 G) mobile network has been introduced on an international scale and has transformed the concept of wireless communication by providing ultra-high data rates, close to zero latency, and seamless connectivity. Nevertheless, its distributed architecture, network slicing, and software-defined settings present new levels of security vulnerability. The current paper suggests a new framework that combines both artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced cryptography schemes to enhance the security of 5 G networks. The core of this strategy is the combination of Q-Learning and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), as Q-Learning is used to dynamically optimize the resource distribution and reduce computational and energy consumption constraints on GANs and other deep neural networks, including autoencoders. This integration improves the ability to respond to emerging attack patterns and detect threats in real time. We also compare the most popular cryptographic methods, post-quantum cryptography, homomorphic encryption, and blockchain-based authentication, with their effectiveness in preventing unauthorized access and data breaches while maintaining 5 G operational performance. These approaches have serious limitations, despite their promise, such as adversarial attack threats, which undermine AI processing of large-scale blockchain data, and the massive computational cost of quantumresistant algorithms. Our results indicate the importance of further improvement of hybrid AI models, such as the QLearning GAN. Smart AI algorithms combined with strong cryptographic techniques will enable 5 G networks in the future to be resilient, scalable, secure, and reliable global communication.

title: Evaluating Communication and Architectural Overheads in NTT Accelerators for ML-KEM
journal: 2026 IEEE 29th International Symposium on Design and Diagnostics of Electronic Circuits and Systems (DDECS)
abs: The standardization of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) has led to the adoption of ML-KEM, a lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber. ML-KEM heavily relies on polynomial multiplication over the Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problem, efficiently implemented using the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT). While the NTT significantly reduces computational complexity, its irregular memory access patterns and high arithmetic intensity pose challenges for efficient software execution, especially in constrained environments. Consequently, hardware acceleration has become essential for enabling practical ML-KEM deployment in embedded and edge systems. Recent research has proposed several hardware accelerators for the NTT, but often without demonstrating their effectiveness in accelerating full matrix-vector products within ML-KEM. Designing such accelerators requires careful architectural trade-offs involving memory organization, data movement, parallelism, and system integration. The main contribution of this paper is a comprehensive assessment of communication, memory arrangement, and architectural overheads in NTT accelerators. We analyze state-of-the-art NTT acceleration techniques for ML-KEM and we propose a hardware architecture optimized for efficient matrixvector multiplication. Our NTT-based accelerator is integrated into a RISC-V System-on-Chip (SoC), and we evaluate the impact of key architectural choices (e.g., parallelism on the butterfly units, latency of communication and memory arrangement) on area and performance.

title: Error Injecting Circuit: An Alternative to Discrete Gaussian Samplers
journal: 2026 IEEE 29th International Symposium on Design and Diagnostics of Electronic Circuits and Systems (DDECS)
abs: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) schemes, such as Learning with Errors (LWE), rely on adding Gaussian noise to arithmetic operations to achieve security against quantum adversaries. Efficient generation of this noise is critical for hardware implementations, particularly in resource-constrained environments like IoT devices. Traditional approaches employ Gaussian samplers to produce discrete Gaussian noise, but these methods introduce significant area overhead and latency, limiting their practical applicability. In this work, we propose a novel hardware architecture that generates Gaussian-like noise using controlled XOR-based bit-flip operations integrated directly into arithmetic circuits. Our approach achieves up to a$3 \times$reduction in area compared to conventional hardware Gaussian samplers, while introducing negligible delay. The resulting architectures provide an efficient and lightweight solution for noise injection, making them highly suitable for deployment in constrained hardware platforms.

title: Granger-Inspired Predictive Structure Test for RBG/RNG Evaluation
journal: 2026 IEEE 19th Dallas Circuits and Systems Conference (DCAS)
abs: New standards for post-quantum cryptography rely on new methods to evaluate the quality of random bit generators. Existing approaches largely rely on correlation-based tests, which are limited in their ability to capture dependence. In particular, they do not directly assess independence or reveal potential cause-and-effect relationships within the sequence. To address this gap, we introduce a methodology for evaluating random generators that draws on the concept of causality as a measure of predictability. We introduce the Granger-inspired Predictive Structure Test, which evaluates subsequences of a bitstream by comparing a logistic regression model against a null model, enabling the detection of predictive dependencies that correlationbased methods overlook. We show that, under assumptions aligning our method with a Granger causality test, the method detects long-term predictive dependencies and identifies nonrandomness at a significantly higher rate than widely used statistical tests.

title: StreamNTT: A High-Throughput, HLS-Based Streaming NTT Accelerator for HBM-Equipped FPGAs
abs: Lattice-based post-quantum cryptography (PQC) relies extensively on the number-theoretic transform (NTT), and large-scale deployments require throughput-optimized accelerators capable of computing thousands of NTTs per session. To address this need, we present StreamNTT, a high-throughput NTT accelerator developed using high-level synthesis (HLS) for field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) equipped with high bandwidth memory (HBM). StreamNTT effectively leverages the parallelism inherent in the NTT by overcoming several obstacles that limit the scalability of streaming dataflow designs. Specifically, we introduce HLS-friendly butterfly units that integrate butterfly computation and reorder buffering into a single pipelined loop. In addition, we propose a butterfly merging strategy that reduces first-in, first-out channels and buffers. Finally, we present a placement-aware instance-level parallelism scheme for FPGA platforms with multiple HBM channels and super logic regions. On the Alveo U280 platform, the proposed optimizations improve throughput by a factor of 7.2 and achieve a speedup of more than 2.7 times compared to state-of-the-art FPGA-based NTT accelerators. As an open-source design, StreamNTT establishes a scalable foundation for advancing high-performance PQC acceleration.

title: Formal Methods-Assisted Chosen Ciphertext Attacks on PQC CRYSTALS-Kyber Using Electromagnetic Emanations
abs: NIST has released a set of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards that address the threat posed by the emergence of quantum computing. The standard includes a modular lattice-based key exchange mechanism (ML-KEM) based on the CRYSTALS-Kyber algorithm. Recent work has shown that Kyber is susceptible to electromagnetic (EM) and power side-channel attacks. A full understanding of the side-channel vulnerabilities in Kyber is of paramount importance for next-generation communication and computing infrastructures.In this study, we target a previously unexplored section of the Kyber algorithm and implement a chosen ciphertext side-channel attack. We focus our attack on the Barrett reduction operation in the decapsulation algorithm. Compared to previous attacks on Barrett reduction, which targeted variables after the Inverse-Number Theoretic Transform (INTT), we focus on Barrett reduction on NTT variables, allowing for more general chosen ciphertexts that can evade input sanity checking. We design a scheme that requires only a set of 12 ciphertexts and side-channel EM traces of the corresponding decapsulation processes, which can reveal distinct leakages under different key values. The secret key is retrieved by pattern matching of the EM leakages. We develop an algorithm that utilizes an SMT solver to automatically select a set of ciphertexts. We implement Kyber on an ARM Cortex M4-based microcontroller and launch this new EM side-channel attack. Our results show that the attack achieves a success rate of over 95% in recovering the secret key value.

title: PQCUARK: A Scalar RISC-V ISA Extension for ML-KEM and ML-DSA
abs: Recent advances in quantum computing pose a threat to the security of digital communications, as large-scale quantum machines can break commonly used public-key cryptographic algorithms. To mitigate this risk, post-quantum cryptography (PQC) schemes are being standardized, with recent NIST recommendations selecting two lattice-based schemes, ML-KEM for key encapsulation and ML-DSA for digital signatures, alongside other schemes. Two computationally intensive kernels dominate the execution of these schemes: the Number-Theoretic Transform (NTT) for polynomial multiplication and theKeccak-f1600permutation function for polynomial sampling and hashing. This paper presents PQCUARK, a scalar RISC-V ISA extension that accelerates these key operations. PQCUARK integrates two novel accelerators within the core pipeline: (i) a packed SIMD butterfly unit capable of performing NTT butterfly operations on 2×32bit or 4×16bit polynomial coefficients, and (ii) a permutation engine that delivers two Keccak rounds per cycle, hosting a private state and a direct interface to the core Load Store Unit, eliminating the need for a custom register file interface. We have integrated PQCUARK into an RV64 core and deployed it on an FPGA. Experimental results demonstrate that PQCUARK provides up to 10.1× speedup over the NIST baselines and 2.3× over the optimized software, and it outperforms similar state-of-the-art approaches between 1.4-12.3× in performance. ASIC synthesis in GF22-FDSOI technology shows a moderate core area increase of 8% at 1.2 GHz, with PQCUARK units being outside the critical path.

title: Multi-Partner Project: Quantum-Secure IoT-based Digital Manufacturing Pilot in QUBIP project
abs: Connectivity has become essential to modern manufacturing, but it also introduces new security challenges. Industrial IoT ecosystems rely on public-key cryptography to protect communications, firmware, and operational data. However, the emergence of quantum computing threatens to undermine these cryptographic foundations, exposing long-lived manufacturing systems to future attacks. This paper presents the Quantum-Secure IoT-based Digital Manufacturing Pilot, developed within the EU-funded QUBIP project, which investigates the integration of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) into IoT environments. The pilot aims to demonstrate how quantum resistant algorithms can be efficiently deployed across heterogeneous devices with limited resources to ensure data exchange and authentication. By combining software and hardware-based approaches, the proposed pilot provides a replicable model for PQC migration in digital manufacturing, ensuring long-term data integrity and resilience in the quantum era.

title: Focus Session: LLM4PQC ─ Accurate and Efficient Synthesis of PQC Cores by Feedback-Driven LLMs
abs: The design of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) hardware is a complex and hierarchical process with many challenges. A primary bottleneck is the conversion of PQC reference codes from C to high-level synthesis (HLS) specifications, which requires extensive manual refactoring[1]─[3]. Another bottleneck is the scalability of synthesis for complex PQC primitives, including number theoretic transform (NTT) accelerators and wide memory interfaces. While large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable results for coding in general-purpose languages like Python, coding for hardware design is more challenging; feedback-driven and agentic integration are key principles of successful state-of-the-art approaches. Here, we propose LLM4PQC, an LLM-based framework that refactors high-level PQC specifications and reference C codes into HLS-ready and synthesizable C code. Our framework generates and verifies the resulting RTL code. For correctness, we leverage a hierarchy of checks, covering fast C compilation and simulation as well as RTL simulation. Case studies on NIST PQC reference designs demonstrate a reduction in manual effort and accelerated design-space exploration compared to traditional flows. Overall, LLM4PQC provides a powerful and efficient pathway for synthesizing complex hardware accelerators.

title: Open-Source Framework for Secure Hardware Design with Simulation-based Leakage Assessment
abs: Side-channel resilience is a critical requirement for cryptographic accelerators. However, current validation approaches rely heavily on costly, measurement-based testing, which is typically applicable only at the final stages of the design flow. This reliance on physical prototypes is aggravated by the lack of integrated security analysis in fragmented toolchains. To address these challenges, we introduce the HWSEC-OSS Framework, a comprehensive open-source platform designed to streamline the security validation of hardware designs. The framework integrates a complete digital design flow with a pre-silicon Side-Channel Analysis (SCA) module based on Hamming-distance power modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework by identifying leakage sources in an EdDSA25519 implementation, exhibiting a strong correlation between simulation-based results and measurements from a physical FPGA prototype. Furthermore, we apply the flow to a hardware implementation of ML-KEM, demonstrating scalability to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). By providing an integrated environment for early security feedback, this work constitutes a fast, cost-effective solution for hardware security validation.

title: CIRCE CROSS Integrated RISC-V Cryptographic Extension
abs: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is moving from algorithm selection to deployment, where performance, energy, and software portability are key constraints, especially on embedded and IoT-class processors. Many PQC schemes stress general-purpose cores with irregular control flow, large arithmetic workloads, and heavy memory traffic. Instruction-set extensions (ISE) and tightly integrated accelerators offer a practical middle ground: they speed up dominant kernels while preserving programmability and avoiding the rigidity of fully fixed-function hardware. In this context, we target post-quantum digital signatures, which remain under active evaluation, including NIST's 2023 call for additional schemes. We focus on CROSS, a code-based signature built from zero-knowledge proofs and the Restricted Syndrome Decoding Problem, and present CIRCE: a RISC-V─integrated extension connected through the Core-V eXtension Interface (CV-X-IF). CIRCE supports both R-SDP and R-SDP(G), runs across all official parameter sets without hardware retuning, and achieves an average 2× speed-up on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA with an ultra-compact footprint (down to 800 LUTs / 100 FFs).

title: MARS: A General GPU Optimization Framework for Merkle-Tree─Enabled Cryptography
abs: Merkle trees underpin diverse cryptographic systems, from hash-based signatures (e.g., LMS, XMSS) to blockchain (e.g., Bitcoin, Ethereum), post-quantum cryptography (e.g., SPHINCS+), and zero-knowledge protocols. Their strength lies in providing efficient verification with compact authentication paths, making them a fundamental primitive in modern cryptographic systems. Existing acceleration of Merkle trees primarily focuses on assigning parallel processing units (e.g., PEs or CUDA cores) to leaf nodes. However, due to the inherent reduction structure, the number of active computations decreases by half at each upper level, leading to progressively lower hardware utilization, especially for trees with greater depth. Furthermore, existing resource allocation strategies for Merkle tree computations rely on heuristic theoretical approximations, which tend to converge to suboptimal configurations. To address these challenges, we propose MARS, a general GPU-based optimization framework1, and use the Merkle tree─intensive FORS (Forest of Random Subset) component in SPHINCS+as a representative case study. MARS leverages the fixed parameters of FORS as guidance to increase the computational load of individual warps, accelerates the tree-reduction process by minimizing shared memory usage and utilizing registers more effectively, and finally, inspired by automated tuning, applies profiling-guided parallel optimization across multiple Merkle trees to achieve architecture-portable configurations. Compared to the latest GPU-optimized FORS signature generation on RTX4090, MARS achieves signature generation throughput improvements of 2.52×, 2.39×and 2.33×under three differentf-parameter sets.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography: From Risks to User Awareness
journal: 2026 13th International Conference on Computing for Sustainable Global Development (INDIACom)
abs: Across modern digital and industrial environments, the rapid growth in publicly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerabilities in recent years has created serious challenges for organizations. Sensitive data faces exposure not only from present-day attacks, but also from future quantum-enabled threats. This threat is intensified by the "harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL)" threat model, in which adversaries capture encrypted data today for future decryption. In response, the current research has divided into three pillars of awareness, assessment, and mitigation. This research focuses on the awareness level, aiming to improve the understanding of quantum-related cyber risks and their impact on critical environments. We depend on the Metaverse to provide more effective and immersive awareness tools. At the mitigation level, the research in this stage just gives practical recommendations that will enhance resilience. Overall, the framework aims at providing an enhanced understanding, simulation, and management of quantum threats in cybersecurity contexts.

title: Quantum Leap in Financial Security: Hybrid Cryptography Approach
journal: 2026 13th International Conference on Computing for Sustainable Global Development (INDIACom)
abs: Many traditional encryption techniques commonly used in financial systems face serious threats from the rapid development of quantum computing. Quantum attacks based on Shor's and Grover's algorithm are effective against the RSA, and ECC methods that secure online banking, digital payments, and interbank communications. To mitigate on this increasing risk, this paper suggests hybrid cryptographic architecture based on symmetric encryption, post-quantum cryptography (PQC), and quantum key distribution (QKD) for secure financial transactions. The Quantum-resistant security significance comes because the financial models produce massive data sets for fraud detection and predictive risk. Not only does it offer the previously unreachable computational capabilities, but also utilizes the potentials of large-scale financial data analytics to make the decision-making process fast and well informed, and in this light, the present research recommends a hybrid cryptographic approach with an integrated security framework for the financial sector that combines symmetric encryption, post-quantum cryptography (PQC), and quantum key distribution (QKD). The proposed structure relies on (1) the quantum-resistance of PQC for resilience and authentication, (2) the information-theoretic security of QKD for key establishment, and (3) the efficacy of symmetric cryptography for protecting high-throughput transactions. The framework covers the short-term practical limitations and long-term quantum risks based on the combined use of quantum and conventional security primitives. This paper points out the role and transformation of digital financial ecosystem in the quantum era by elaborating challenges, opportunities and future of quantum cryptography in the banking industry.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Cybersecurity in 5G and 6G Networks: SDN, NFV, Slicing, and Massive IoT Security
journal: 2026 13th International Conference on Computing for Sustainable Global Development (INDIACom)
abs: The advancement from 5G through 6G networks has brought sophisticated new features like network softwarization, virtualization and intelligent automation, while at the same time increasing the surface area of cybersecurity dangers. This paper provides a high-level insight in clearly presenting a thorough review of all security challenges in Software-Defined Networking (SDN), Network Function Virtualization (NFV) and network slicing and massive Internet of Things (IoT) deployments in next generation networks.
